subsubtopic: INCREASE IN PRIVATE AIRCRAFT PARKING FEES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in May of 1982 the Department of Transport levied a 350 per cent increase on parking fees for private aircraft at DOT airports. Only six weeks later the six and five formula was introduced by the Government as a check on inflation. The imposition of a further 6 per cent as of May this year in these fees means in reality that a tax of an extra 21 per cent has been levied on the rate in existence just a year ago. This is not the true six and five approach, nor does it take into account the additional 6 per cent to be imposed on landing fees for private aircraft, fuel concession fees, and on international route fees.
Furthermore, the Department has yet to allow those paying an annual parking fee at one airport to park, without paying an extra fee, at a nearby airport when weather or other landing conditions prevent a pilot from reaching his home base.
Most private operators are businessmen selling Canadian products continent-wide and keeping Canadians at work. Why are they being asked to carry this additional heavy burden, along with a radio operator's fee that costs twice as much as a radio licence for sports boats and, indeed, for cargo carriers on the Great Lakes?

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Hudecki (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS SOUGHT BY PART-TIME UNIVERSITY STUDENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there are approximately 250,000 part-time university students in Canada, many of whom attend McMaster University and Mohawk College in Hamilton. These part-time students form a rapidly growing sector of the post-secondary educational community. As such, they are concerned with amending the Income Tax Act in order to assist this movement to part-time studies in a more
equitable way, and to permit part-time students to qualify in principle and on a pro-rata basis for some of the tax exemptions now available only to full-time students.
The amendments which the Canadian Organization of Parttime University Students is proposing to the Income Tax Act include pro-rating the $50 a month educational deduction; transferring the tuition deduction from a non-working spouse to a working spouse; and allowing part-time students to deduct incidental fees.
Since we live in an age of constant and rapid change, people must continually upgrade their education and most can do this only on a part-time basis. That being the case, I suggest that we at the federal level should do all we can to encourage Canadians to upgrade their educational level through parttime study in order that they may acquire the skills they will need for the jobs of the future.

subsubtopic: RATE OF FARM BANKRUPTCIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, farm bankruptcy statistics were issued this week for the first quarter of 1983, and comparisons were made with the first quarter of 1982. On a national basis there was no great change. Bankruptcies in 1983 amounted to 115 compared to 113, but we see a great difference or shift, if you will, in the bankruptcies on a regional basis. We note that in western Canada bankruptcies increased from 17 a year ago to 39 this year, a dramatic increase of 130 per cent.
While in some regions of the country the bankruptcy rate has remained about the same, the Government has not paid any attention to the increase in bankruptcies in the areas hardest hit. Indeed, the response has been to ignore them. The initial prices for wheat have dropped in the area where bankruptcies are now the highest, and the Government is intending to increase freight rates in that area as well. Again, the result will be to reduce net incomes and further increase and aggravate the probability of bankruptcy in that region. subtopic: ANNOUNCED CLOSURE OF REFINERY AT HOLYROOD, NFLD.

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: ANNOUNCED CLOSURE OF REFINERY AT HOLYROOD, NFLD.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on March 30, 1983, Ultramar Canada announced it was closing its refinery at Holyrood, Newfoundland, as of June 30. This will mean the loss of 105 man years of employment and an approximate loss of $91 million to the Newfoundland gross provincial product.
When this refinery was opened in 1960 it provided Ultramar with access to and a toe hold in the North American market. While this was only a small refinery with a 15,000 barrel a day capacity, production has been reduced to less than 50 per cent because of a falloff in the demand for heavy crude as a result of the change in the energy pattern with respect to home heating fuel consumption and so on.
My point is that the closing of the Holyrood refinery, Madam Speaker, is a direct result of the expansion of Ultra-mar's refinery in Quebec. I do not quarrel with that, but that expansion has been at the expense of Newfoundland's refinery, and I believe Ultramar has a responsibility to Newfoundland because it was through the people and Government of that Province that its owners got their introduction to the North American market in the first instance. However, they indicate their decision is final and irrevocable, so I want to suggest, through this procedure, that the Government of Canada, through the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien), and the Minister of DREE, should get in touch with the Government of Newfoundland with a view to taking whatever steps are necessary to keep the Holyrood refinery open.

subtopic: PARLIAMENTARY PRESS GALLERY-STIPULATIONS GOVERNING BUDGET COVERAGE
PARLIAMENTARY PRESS GALLERY-STIPULATIONS GOVERNING BUDGET COVERAGE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, George Orwell's Big Brother 1984 has obviously arrived eight months early. I refer to the Minister of Finance's new rules governing the nation's news media on budget night next Tuesday. Madam Speaker, I spent some 20 years in the Parliamentary Press Gallery, one of them as that Association's President under the current Liberal Prime Minister. I can tell him and this House that I have never experienced such blatant news management by any Canadian Government.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and his Liberal advisers are telling the Parliamentary Press Gallery who can report the budget, when they can report the budget, and how they can report the budget. That constitutes "news management at best, censorship at worst", to quote commentator Bruce Phillips.
The Liberal Government is now decreeing who will be considered journalists, and who will be accredited as economic experts and analysts to be allowed into the traditional budget
lock-up. In addition, the Liberal Government is now insisting that the media, under signed undertaking, will for the first time remain locked up in the Government Conference Centre for one full hour after the Minister begins his budget address at 8 p.m. EST. This will drastically affect national television and radio reporting and analysis of the budget.
Basically, this is being done to keep off the air those journalists and experts who might dare criticize the budget while the Minister intones his address.
I appeal to the Government of Canada to revert to the traditional practice of covering budgets, and to trust members of the media, along with Members of Parliament, to observe those traditional guidelines. Above all, I urge the Government to prevent this outrage to freedom of the press.

subtopic: PROTEST AGAINST ARRANGEMENTS FOR MEDIA COVERAGE OF BUDGET
PROTEST AGAINST ARRANGEMENTS FOR MEDIA COVERAGE OF BUDGET
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as Canadians await the 1983 budget, a budget coming at a time when the state of the Canadian economy is at its lowest ebb since the 1930s, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) has been making a number of efforts in the last number of months to consult with various Canadians in various regions of Canada. However, already a dark pall is beginning to form over the budget process. We find that the Minister of Finance is now concerned about the critics who will be commenting on the budget, both in the media as well as in the Opposition Parties and, as a result, is taking steps to, in a sense, muzzle reaction on the eve of the budget.
Surely the budget itself should stand on its own merits. If the Government has confidence in the Minister of Finance and his budget, it ought to have no concern over Opposition Members or the media making positive criticisms of its budget statement. Therefore, I urge the Minister of Finance to reconsider the procedures on budget night in terms of keeping Opposition critics as well as media critics from responding as early as traditionally has been done on the night of a budget. I urge him to remember that this is the most important budget which the country will receive for the next number of years and it is imperative that fair and objective criticism be presented.

subsubtopic: LOSS OF JOBS AT SAINT JOHN, N.B.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the past 15 months some 32 full-time Canadian Pacific Railway clerical positions in the Customer Service Centre and the West Side wharf in Saint John, New Brunswick, have been lost. This has resulted in a general deterioration of rail service and now poses a threat to the welfare of the good citizens of Saint John.
April 15, 1983

Four of the workers who lost their jobs were inter-change clerks who would know the exact location of cars carrying dangerous goods passing through the city. With the elimination of the clerical jobs, the possibility of dangerous commodities travelling through the city unchecked, or their exact location unknown, greatly increases.
Additionally, there would be no personal contact between the fire officials and the railway regarding the passage of these goods and the event of disaster heightened by delayed response time.
As the Government appears to have some influence over the operations of the Canadian Pacific Railway by the fact it can bind CPR workers to the six and five wage program by law, I would urge the Government to discuss with CPR officials the possibility of rehiring the inter-change clerks to assure the exact locations of dangerous commodities are known and reported.
Rail operations in Saint John have been whittled down to mere bones resulting in extensive lay-offs in all areas of rail transportation, and poorer service. I would urge CPR to cease lay-offs that not only affect the quality of rail services in Saint John and New Brunswick but force workers into positions of unemployment, unknown futures, and despair.

subsubtopic: CANADAIR-DEAL WITH ARGUS CORPORATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it has been publically alleged that Canadair gave a private jet to the Argus Corporation, and the allegation has not yet been denied. It is also well known that the President of Argus is Conrad Black.
Furthermore, according to Peter Newman in his book "The Establishment Man", Conrad Black last year hired as his private consultant the former private secretary to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), now on his second try as Liberal candidate for Spadina.
Considering the Prime Minister's often stated concern to discourage conflict of interest, it would be helpful if the Prime Minister would inquire, and make public, whether Jim Coutts helped to arrange the sweetheart deal between Canadair and Argus.

subsubtopic: CROWSNEST PASS RATE-GOVERNMENT ADVERTISING IN SUPPORT OF CHANGES
speechtext:

Oral Questions
Would the Minister confirm whether it is the intention of the Government of Canada to insert a four-page supplement in Canada's daily newspapers next week to promote the Government's legislation to dismantle the Crow? If it is, could the Minister tell us why this is being done before the legislation has been introduced in the House of Commons, and under whose authority is the supplement being inserted? As well, can he give the House some indication of whether or not it will be included in all the dailies across Canada, and at what cost?
Are we also to assume that the Government is contemplating a corresponding television promotion as well, along the lines of the flying Canadian geese that we witnessed about a year ago, aptly substituted with a flock of crows departing from the Canadian agricultural scene?

Madam Speaker, it is a long question. Yes indeed, we are contemplating that. I have a copy here which I could show the Hon. Member. It will appear this weekend.
The reason it appears before the Bill is something that I cannot control. There are deadlines over which I am not the master.
Its cost is approximately $350,000. It will appear in a number of papers, in English only, because we already have some in French. It will appear in a number of regions in Canada.

subsubtopic: CROWSNEST PASS RATE-GOVERNMENT ADVERTISING IN SUPPORT OF CHANGES
speechtext: The same message?

The Government is sponsoring it, but presumably I take some responsibility for what is in there. I feel this is quite defensible. If standards are important in these matters, which I think they are. So I am in very good company.

subsubtopic: CROWSNEST PASS RATE-GOVERNMENT ADVERTISING IN SUPPORT OF CHANGES
speechtext:
Hear, hear!

April 15, 1983

speechtext: Unfortunately, the ad fails to recognize the impact that the Pepin proposals will have upon the producers of Canada in terms of grain production and the over-all economic hardships that it will impose upon the producers of Canada.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT FARMERS BE PROVIDED WITH ADVERTISING FUNDS
REQUEST THAT FARMERS BE PROVIDED WITH ADVERTISING FUNDS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, in the interest of fairness and maintaining a balance, would the Minister support the farmers of Canada in running a corresponding ad telling their side of the story and the disincentives that this will have on the producers and the economic impact it will have upon them? Will he support the farmers of western Canada by providing funds for a corresponding ad which would add some balance to the debate?

subtopic: REQUEST THAT FARMERS BE PROVIDED WITH ADVERTISING FUNDS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will not have to support them because they already do it. For example, the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool has been running an ad throughout the country addressing itself to Members of Parliament from different areas, and pleading with them not to agree with the Bill when it is introduced.
At the end of the day, I think this is educational. The public is entitled to receive different points of view. In the final analysis it is the taxpayer, be he or she a member of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, a citizen of Saskatchewan or of the country as a whole, who pays for it. Presumably they do not mind being educated in this fashion.

Madam Speaker, unfortunately it is very difficult for the pools, farm organizations and producer groups to compete with the treasury of the federal Government. I repeat that this is an advertising campaign being conducted for legislation that is yet to be introduced in the House of Commons.
Having looked at the ad, I note that the supplement emphasizes job creation, high technology, and economic stimulus, with very little mention of the impact on the producers of Canada. Are we to assume that this package represents the Government's new economic strategy? Is this the Government's megaproject for the 1980s? Can we expect the Minister of Finance, in the introduction of his budget, to emphasize correspondingly the dismantling of the Crow as the Government's megaproject for the 1980s?

Madam Speaker, that is not a bad idea. It is indeed a megaproject, if ever there was one, at $16.5 billion over the next eight or nine years. That is not a bad contribution to the economy. It is certainly a very strong contribution, which the Minister of Finance has said a number of times, to the recovery that we are witnessing now. From that point of view, I thank the Hon.
Member for making a contribution to the publicity we are trying to give it. It is not a description of the Bill. But there is in each ad a short enumeration of what will be the main parts of the Bill. I shall say more on that as soon as I can.

Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Transport. In the advertising on the Crow rate there seems to be, as the Hon. Member for Vegreville pointed out, a definite absence of the benefit to the farmers. The advertisement clearly indicates the benefits to the rail system. The Minister will know, by the multitude of letters that have crossed his desk, that there is absolutely no consensus for the type of advertising that is taking place.
Will the Minister consider exactly what is happening to the producer? Will he look at the cost to the producer at a time when world grain prices have dropped $1 a bushel? Will the Minister consider the increased costs of production? The farmers cannot accept the increased costs that are being advertised in the Pepin proposal at this time.

Madam Speaker, Hon. Members will have plenty of opportunity to debate each one of those points. The benefits that farmers will gain from this proposal are pretty easy to enumerate. For the first time farmers will have certainty about the transportation of grain. Farmers worry every year whether grain will get to the coast on time. Farmers will not have to worry any more because they will have the best freight transportation system in the world.
Farmers will be able to save on storage and demurrage. Farmers will be allowed to diversify their crops and will be allowed to process more than they are now. What farmers will pay in return, on the other side of the equation, will remain quite moderate, in my view.
What the Crow represents now is a cost of 2.5 per cent of the price of grain internationally. If this system that we will introduce goes through, in four or five years from now it will represent 5 per cent of the cost of grain internationally. At the end of the decade it will represent 8 per cent, 9 per cent or 10 per cent, depending upon a number of factors that I cannot predict entirely accurately. If that is so, 8 per cent to 10 per cent will be about the average of the last 30 years and this percentage will be substantially less than it has been at different times in the history of the country, because at different times the cost has represented 30 per cent or 40 per cent of the price of grain. I will have plenty of occasions on which to spoonfeed my friends on these facts of grain life, and I will be delighted to do so.

subtopic: IMPACT OF PROPOSED CHANGES ON CENTRAL CANADA
IMPACT OF PROPOSED CHANGES ON CENTRAL CANADA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a further question for the Minister of Transport. The Minister knows that in this proposal there is a 500 per cent increase in cost to farmers. He also knows that by 1992 the average
April 15, 1983

farmer will pay at least $8,000 more for freight transportation than he is paying now. Farmers are concerned about where they will raise the $8,000 at a time when the price of grain is failling. There seems to be a direct parallel to the national energy policy here with no consideration to the field, with no consideration to the producer, and with no consideration to production.
For the welfare of all of Canada, what is the Minister going to do if he has bankrupt farmers on his hands who will not be able to buy combines and tractors from central Canada, and who will not be able to buy rubber and steel from central Canada? Has the Minister considered the impact of such a loss to all Canada in the Pepin proposals?

subtopic: IMPACT OF PROPOSED CHANGES ON CENTRAL CANADA
speechtext: Madam Speaker, there is much to be said on this subject. The Hon. Member used the figure of 500 per cent. Five hundred per cent of what? A better way to say it is that, under the proposal we will introduce, the farmer will pay two times Crow in four years, which is a change from 13 cents per bushel to 26 cents per bushel. At the end of the decade he might pay, because there are so many factors, 75 cents per bushel.

subtopic: IMPACT OF PROPOSED CHANGES ON CENTRAL CANADA
speechtext: That is 500 per cent.

subtopic: IMPACT OF PROPOSED CHANGES ON CENTRAL CANADA
speechtext: Even by your math that is 500 per cent.

subtopic: IMPACT OF PROPOSED CHANGES ON CENTRAL CANADA
speechtext: It is less than the cost of a stamp on an envelope that goes to Canada Post today.

subtopic: IMPACT OF PROPOSED CHANGES ON CENTRAL CANADA
speechtext: That is going up too.

subtopic: IMPACT OF PROPOSED CHANGES ON CENTRAL CANADA
speechtext: It is going up, but I predict that it will never go up further than the price of a stamp on an envelope.

subtopic: IMPACT OF PROPOSED CHANGES ON CENTRAL CANADA
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: IMPACT OF PROPOSED CHANGES ON CENTRAL CANADA
speechtext: You will regret those words.

subtopic: IMPACT OF PROPOSED CHANGES ON CENTRAL CANADA
speechtext:
There must be a comparison there which should impress my hon. friend.
Anyway, by way of comparison, during the Saskatchewan election a certain Minister of Agriculture was telling the people, "Beware of the Pepin plan-13 times Crow". Well, it is two times Crow in four years' time and will be five times Crow at the end of the decade. I forgot to mention, of course, all kinds of possibilities. There is no doubt the farmer will be able to produce, not only with the assurance that his grain will be transported, but will be able to produce a lot more than he produces now.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Transport as well. What right does the Government have to run a four-page tabloid like this one, in at least ten Ontario papers tomorrow? The Crow legislation has not even been
Oral Questions
introduced into the House of Commons. We have not even had first reading of the Bill. There was no reference to it in the Throne Speech. There was no reference to it whatsoever in the Estimates. There was no promise made of it whatsoever in the 1980 Liberal election platform. What right does the Government have to spend this amount of public money, without the consent of Parliament, on what is clearly a partisan ad on behalf of the Liberal Party of something which has not even come before the House?
Madam Speaker, I have already answered that question in the first answer I gave. The rights are the same as the ones which the NDP Government of Saskatchewan was using some months ago.
Oh, oh!

It is all in here. I think we have to admit that they are quite frank about it, "Paid by the Transportation Agency of the Government of Saskatchewan." It could not be any clearer. Not only is this proselytizing before the Bill was even announced, this is also indulging people in the wrong belief that it would be 13 times Crow. My hon. friend obviously has two standards-one for his Party and one for the rest of the world, or one for his Province and one for the rest of Canada.
As usual, the Minister of Transport is once again misleading the House.
Oh, oh!
The advertising in Saskatchewan was based upon legislative authority in that Province. It was approved by the Legislature of Saskatchewan, and that has not happened in this case.

Madam Speaker, Government Members have access to public funds which we in the Opposition do not have; we cannot spend money like that. I want to know whether or not the Minister of Transport will now withdraw these ads, or whether or not he will have the guts to have the Liberal Party of Canada reimburse the Government of Canada and the taxpayers of Canada for these partisan political ads.

It was
within the authority of the NDP Government of Saskatchewan to send the bill to the Transportation Agency, a Crown corporation of the Government of Saskatchewan. No, Madam Speaker, I think Governments must tell the country what they intend to do. That is the normal process. As my hon. friend knows, we have had a few Members for a while in the West now, explaining the Bill. I do my very best and my colleagues do their very best to do that. But the use of newspapers is one

April 15, 1983
Oral Questions
of the normal, natural, sensible and moral ways of taking information to the public.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT TRANSPORT RATES BE TIED TO GRAIN EXPORT PRICES
REQUEST THAT TRANSPORT RATES BE TIED TO GRAIN EXPORT PRICES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister of Transport a couple of supplementary questions. He said that the cost of the movement of grain would not rise any more than the cost of a postage stamp. Is he also making other parallels that the kind of service will be analogous to that provided by the Post Office?
The minister makes reference to the increased cost projected to the year 2000 being somewhere in the eight per cent range of the export sale price for grain. Will the Minister undertake at least one measure which will give farm producers some security by tying transportation cost to a percentage of the export price for grain, rather than tying it to prices which reflect inflation as in the cost of transport, because farmers cannot cause or protect themselves from inflationary factors?

subtopic: REQUEST THAT TRANSPORT RATES BE TIED TO GRAIN EXPORT PRICES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the service that the railways will give is the type that the Post Office would like to give, so both of them meet in their desire for excellence. On the subject, and it is a very popular one I may say, of tying the cost of transportation to the selling price of grain, this idea is growing in popularity in the West. I must say, and my Hon. friend knows because he is quite learned on this, that the subject was not brought forward with any degree of intensity in the Gilson exercise, and that it regrettable.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT TRANSPORT RATES BE TIED TO GRAIN EXPORT PRICES
speechtext: Exercise?

subtopic: REQUEST THAT TRANSPORT RATES BE TIED TO GRAIN EXPORT PRICES
speechtext: I am sorry that I do not have the whole lexicon of my hon. friend at my command. The subject was not brought up at the Gilson group committee, or call it whatever you want. I was saying that it is an idea that has some importance. This Government, the Members of it and the Members of the Liberal Party are democratic. If there should be a great popular demand for it, if groups which have difficulty accepting this or that part of the program, come together in a very great movement of enthusiasm, I am quite sure the Government will not be indifferent to them.

Madam Speaker, on that narrow section of the whole Crow debate, I say to the Minister that if he searches widely across the Prairies he will find increasing support for the view of tying the cost of the shipment of grain to the export value. It need not be to any one specific year. It could be to a range of years, knowing what happened with the fixed rate in the 1930s when the cost of shipment went to 35 per cent of the price of the grain.
In several responses, once today and previously in the press, the Minister has said that the new Crow rate will save the farmers from demurrage charges. Can he expand on how they can save on demurrage charges from an improved transport system?

Madam Speaker, very simply by getting there on time. If you get to port in a lower number of days, obviously you are in a much better position to serve the ships waiting there. That is a normal consideration. On the previous subject, I know that my hon. friend is campaigning in favour of the Bill which we will introduce. I know he is favourable toward it. I would be grateful if, sometime in a week or so from now, he tells me that on the tying idea he has the wholehearted support of the whole of the Conservative Party and would gladly commit himself to approve the Bill if there was a possibility of including that part.

subsubtopic: DRUMHELLER INSTITUTION-IMPOSITION OF NEW DUTY ROSTER SYSTEM
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Solicitor General. He was here a minute ago. I believe he is behind the curtain.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: DRUMHELLER INSTITUTION-IMPOSITION OF NEW DUTY ROSTER SYSTEM
speechtext: Order. Will the Hon. Member ask his question, and perhaps a Parliamentary Secretary can answer it?

subsubtopic: DRUMHELLER INSTITUTION-IMPOSITION OF NEW DUTY ROSTER SYSTEM
speechtext: The morale among the staff in many of our federal prisons is running very low. If nothing is done we could have a very serious situation on our hands. In the Drumheller penitentiary feelings have reached the explosive stage. One of the aggravations is the imposition by decree of a new duty roster. Why is the Government forcing a new duty roster on the prison staff when the present duty roster and squad system is working to the satisfaction of not only the prison staff but of the administration in the Drumheller Institution?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bob Kaplan (Solicitor General of Canada):
subsubtopic: DRUMHELLER INSTITUTION-IMPOSITION OF NEW DUTY ROSTER SYSTEM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there is a very easy answer to that question. I am doing it because the present duty roster system, in spite of what the Hon. Member says, does not serve the best interests of the prison. It produces a great deal of overtime costs. I hope that the Hon. Member, as a representative of the taxpayers, will be as concerned as I am about that. It also produces periods in which there are less than the proper number of people on regular duty in the institution.
The duty roster system which I have supported, and which is being put into effect this week in Drumheller, will be a much more efficient and effective one. I would urge the Hon. Member to support it. It has already been introduced in Quebec and Ontario. The institution in the Hon. Member's constituency
April 15, 1983

will benefit from having this improved system, and the taxpayers have a great deal to gain from it as well.

subsubtopic: DRUMHELLER INSTITUTION-IMPOSITION OF NEW DUTY ROSTER SYSTEM
speechtext: I suggest to the Minister that the new system will cost more and cause a great deal of disturbance among the staff. It will cost the taxpayer more money. This can be proved by past experience.

Is the Minister aware that enacting this new roster unilaterally is contrary to the agreement the Government has with the staff? Is the Government going to continue to have these things done unilaterally by a few bureaucrats rather than negotiating with the prison staff? Will the Minister hold this up for two weeks so that the prison staff have some opportunity to negotiate? Apparently he is not prepared to do that. Why the rush to shove something down their throats, when the present system is working?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bob Kaplan (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am not willing to give another two weeks before implementing this system because we have already given three months in which there has been a lot of consultation and discussion. The union said it could come up with an equally effective and efficient system, and then was unable to do so. The Member speculates that this will cost the Government more. I can assure him that it will cost the Government less.
Insofar as unrest is concerned, the Hon. Member can have a role to play in that. If he looks at the positive effect that this is having in other institutions where it has been introduced without difficulty, and looks at other penitentiary systems of the Provinces, some of which have been using this system for years, the system that we are now introducing, he will see that it is an advantageous system. The only down side of it, if I can put it that way to the Member, is that some employees who have been getting a lot of overtime will get somewhat less overtime.

subsubtopic: CANADAIR-INQUIRY RESPECTING TASK FORCE REPORT ON FINANCIAL LIABILITIES

That this House condemns the Government for its outright rejection of the sound economic advice given by the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops, and the Government's refusal to adopt the specific recommendations for alternative industrial strategies and the increased community ownership and control of industries where desirable.
He said: Madam Speaker, I believe that it is worth noting that this particular motion comes essentially on the eve of the 1983 budget. What we are doing here today is debating a statement that the Catholic Bishops made a number of weeks ago which reflected on the state of the Canadian economy and presented, from their perspective, a number of solutions. I believe, as conscientious, responsible Members of Parliament,
Supply
that we ought to give this statement some consideration. That is essentially the explanation of my motive for bringing forward this Opposition motion for debate today.
I believe we should congratulate the Conference of Catholic Bishops for its report entitled "Ethical Reflections on the Economic Crisis", for a crisis it certainly is, and ethical reflections are certainly in order. With two million people presently unemployed in Canada, and many more being threatened with the possibility of job loss and lay-offs due in large part to Government policies, I believe that the situation involves not only an economic problem but, indeed, a moral problem as well.
There has been a great deal to say about the world situation in terms of the economic challenges facing western industrialized nations. There has been a feeling articulated from many quarters of Canadian society that the present situation is something which we must indeed accept, that we must tolerate it, that this status quo situation is something with which Canadians must learn to live, and that therefore the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), when he brings in his budget, must stay the course, must not do anything of any radical nature, "radical" meaning a major stimulus to the economy in one sector or another, or taking some dramatic and major action in terms of kick-starting our economy back to life.
I think it must be said at the outset that the problems being faced by Canadians today, in terms of the unemployment albatross which we find around our necks, and which is retarding efforts at economic recovery, are not the same as the situations one finds in all countries. I believe that it is not unreasonable to compare a country such as our own with countries such as Japan and Sweden, not that their solutions are directly applicable here in Canada or that their problems are the same as ours, but because our economies have some similarities.
I note with interest that not many months ago virtually a state of emergency was declared on the island of Japan because the unemployment rate had soared to the unbelievable and unacceptable level of 2.7 per cent. The Japanese Government said that this could go no further, that action must be taken of an emergency nature to stop the search toward these high unemployment levels. The Japanese know that with high levels of unemployment, economic recovery is impossible. This is something that Canadians, by and large, have ignored in our discussions of economic recovery.
Presumably, we assume that economic recovery can occur when two million out of a work force of 12 million are presently unemployed. I, for one, do not believe that that is the case. The Members of my Party believe that economic recovery is virtually impossible with this burden and weight upon our economic shoulders. We feel that now is the time to address this situation head-on in terms of identifying unemployment as an area of virtual preoccupation around this budget.
While inflation is important, and our fight against inflation must never cease, to put all our energies, to focus all our attention on fighting inflation, would be attention and energy

misdirected to a certain extent. Surely, stagflation is our challenge today as opposed to simply inflation. Again, I refer to the country of Sweden, a country not unlike Canada, other than its size. However, the strength of its economy is based by and large on natural resources, a talented population and available capital. Again, that country decided that it was reaching a state of crisis when its unemployment levels had surged to 3 per cent. The realization existed in that country that drastic measures had to be introduced to reverse this trend. Those are progressive steps and ideas. They are countries which put the welfare of their people as their highest priority.
That is essentially what the Catholic Bishops have said. Our Judeo-Christian traditions are based on the principles of respect for the human person, caring and compassion. These principles are practised not only by helping the victims of misfortune but also by attempting to eliminate the causes of this misfortune. The Bishops have essentially asked a fundamentally valid question that we should also be asking here. They asked: do we see society as a machine for the generation of wealth and individual Canadians as mere cogs in that machine, or should our economic activity and production of wealth have as their primary goal the well-being of Canadian citizens?
The Bishops see economic activity as the way to achieve social justice and they consider that economic development can be used to guarantee a level of well-being and dignity for every citizen. Alternatively, others see it quite differently. They view economic activity as a battlefield and an area where the survival of the fittest is the name of the game in which the strong survive and the weak fall.
Since the Bishops made their comment, I have listened to one corporate leader and business lobbyist after another either strongly or quietly condemn the Bishops' position and their involvement in this discussion. These businessmen see our economy as a battlefield where the strong survive and the rich deserve all they have, and that the poor and unemployed are in that position by and large as a result of their own fault. This is simply good nineteenth century laissez-faire economics. There is not anything particularly new about this philosophy but when applied to the 1980s, it is somewhat outmoded. The businessmen believe that, while certain measures must be taken to keep people from rioting in the streets, the status quo must be maintained at all costs and the ratio of rich to poor must not be altered.
What is the ratio? Let us recognize that the top 20 per cent in our country receive 42.5 per cent of total personal income while the bottom 20 per cent receive 4.1 per cent of income. As the Economic Council of Canada identified recently, the gap between the most and least affluent in Canada is growing. In other words, like the gap between the rich and poor nations, the gap between the rich and poor Canadian continues to increase in spite of the good intentions of various levels of Government.
Between 1970 and 1977, wealthy Canadians saw their wealth increased by 3.5 per cent and their debts decreased by 6 per cent. On the other hand, the neediest saw their wealth shrink by 13 per cent and their debt jump by 32 per cent. The Economic Council of Canada suggests that the combination of high interest rate policies and unemployment that has marked the 1980s threatens to accentuate this disparity even further in the years ahead.
I think the best analogy to describe how Canadians have traditionally approached our economy over the years is to consider a poor family in Canada today. This family consists of a father, mother and four children. Perhaps the father, being the sole income earner, has been laid off for a number of months and the family is now finding itself facing welfare as its UI benefits are exhausted. They decide that the way out of this malaise is to focus their attention on the eldest son and make family sacrifices so that he may perhaps obtain a further education which will enable him to succeed in society. He will then look after the rest of the family in later years. To accomplish this the family will have to make sacrifices, such as providing less food for some of the children and providing less funds to help them in their educational pursuits and general lifestyle. All the attention will be focused on the eldest son.
I believe that this is not an uncommon approach taken by Canadian families, and it is certainly an approach that we see taken with the Canadian economy whereby we tend to focus on a few members in society largely at the expense of the rest of society with the assumption that eventually there will be a trickling down of the good life. It is an assumption that after the wealthy few, or the catered to son, succeeds the rest of the family or society will be the beneficiaries.
We have seen this in recent legislation in the House. In recent weeks we passed legislation which will substantially reduce the marginal tax rates for upper income earners while the marginal tax rates for low income and middle income earners will remain about the same. In fact, they will pay slightly more because of the six and five program and the deindexing attached to it. Those upper income earners in society who earn over $100,000 will see a substantial drop in their tax rates. They will have more money to take home or to invest.
When one studies the Income Tax Act of Canada one has to agree that the loopholes-I will not argue about their positive or negative impact-are by and large designed to cater to the upper income earner. The average Canadian citizen has his or her tax deducted at source and there is very little opportunity to use the Canadian tax system to defer taxes or use it for investment purposes. Therefore, again our tax system caters to the upper income earner.
The Bishops have challenged some of the assumptions we have made about how we deal with our economy. Like many, they have recognized that the Canadian economy is going through a period of dynamic transition. Our economy went down a year and a half ago, and whenever it rebounds in the months ahead, if it does, it will emerge in a different form. The structural changes which have occurred in our economy have
April 15, 1983

meant that the many jobs which have been lost will never return, and new and different jobs will emerge. The economy which we have come to know in Canada will be quite different in 10 years or 15 years from now. This process of rapid and dynamic change is like standing on the beach and being beaten by the surf while the sand is washing past and one is sinking down.
The world around us is changing, but I wonder if we are aware of that change? I still hear people from most sectors of the economy and most regions of Canada saying that the economy is recovering and that it has bottomed out. Yet most Canadians see no evidence of this. I therefore wonder if we are grasping at straws and if, as parliamentarians, we want to believe that the economy is recovering and conditions are improving when it may not be so and the pain and human tragedy that over two million Canadians are experiencing will continue in this country for many years.
The Bishops say we have to work to change that and we have to implement strategies that are different from those we have used in the past. When you look at our past performance, it has been dismal. We have not addressed the critical issues facing the country.
I want to mention briefly, to remind us all, just what the Bishops said. Let me quote from their statement as follows:
In developing strategies for economic recovery, we firmly believe that first priority must be given to the real victims of the current recession, namely-the unemployed, the welfare poor, the working poor-pensioners, native peoples, women, young people-and small farmers, fishermen, some factory workers, and some small-businessmen and women. This option calls for economic policies which realize that the needs of the poor have priority over the wants of the rich; that the rights of workers are more important than the maximization of profits; that the participation of marginalized groups takes precedence over the preservation of a system which excludes them.
In other words, a totally new approach to economic recovery than we are presently launching in this country is needed.
The statement continues:
First, unemployment rather than inflation, should be recognized as the number one problem to be tackled in overcoming the present crisis.
The Bishops do not say that inflation should be ignored or seriously combated. They say that inflation should not be our number one priority at the expense of two million plus unemployed.
The Bishops go on to say:
Second, an industrial strategy should be developed to create permanent and meaningful jobs for people in local communities. To be effective, such a strategy should be designed at both national and regional levels.
In other words, obviously we should have a strategy of cooperation between the federal Government and the provincial Governments, and perhaps even the subregional Governments of Canada.
The Bishops' statement continues:
It should include emphasis on increased production, creation of new labour intensive industries for basic needs, and measures to ensure job security for workers.
Supply
Third, a more balanced and equitable program should be developed for reducing and stemming the rate of inflation.
The Bishops wrote that this requires shifting the burden for wage controls to others. In other words, let us not continue to fight inflation by and large on the backs of average working Canadians, but shift this burden to include upper income earners and introduce controls on prices and new forms of taxes on investment income, such as income from dividends and interest. The Bishops' report goes on:
Fourth, greater emphasis should be given to the goal of social responsibility in the current recession.
After all, these are the people out in the trenches. These are the people who are talking to the hard pressed, and who have been working with those who have paid the greatest price.
I go on to quote:
This means that every effort must be made to curtail cut-backs in social services, maintain adequate health care and social security benefits, and above all, guarantee special assistance for the unemployed, welfare recipients, the working poor and one-industry towns suffering from plant shut-downs.
Fifth, labour unions should be asked to play a more decisive and responsible role in developing strategies for economic recovery and employment. This requires the restoration of collective bargaining rights where they have been suspended, collaboration between unions and the unemployed and unorganized workers, and assurances that labour unions will have an effective role in developing economic policies.
Earlier in my speech I referred to Japan and Sweden, two countries that I suggest Canada may take a look at in terms of how they have been working to resolve their economic difficulties.

speechtext:
Both Japan and Sweden recognize that organized labour and unorganized labour play a very critical part in recovery programs. They work to make commitments to meet that particular relationship and to encourage it.
In closing, let me say that we are in the midst of far reaching economic changes. I think we would all agree that new economic vision is needed as well as new tools, new approaches, new methods and new institutions at this time. Something has to be done. Many politicians seem to be tired and uncertain about the realities of our present situation. Business leaders have been prisoners of their own rhetoric, blaming workers for their excessive expectations and declines in the work ethic. Academic economists, secure in their tenure, play computer games and manipulate abstract numbers instead of facing the tragedies of the real world.
The Bishops have issued a challenge, to Canadians and Parliamentarians alike, Mr. Speaker. Let us hope that we can find it within ourselves in this year to face the reality of the unemployment situation and to do something about it.

similar to our own. Sweden's unemployment rate is somewhat higher than Japan's but Sweden has a very distinctly different way of dealing with these problems and its society is structured differently from Canada's. The situation in Sweden is to have very large, national labour organizations, but Sweden's approach has been to impose wage controls and to ensure, as a public policy, that inflation will exceed the increase in wage gains. It is a conscious policy to impose real wage losses on the citizens of Sweden.
On the other hand, Japan has company unions, not industrial unions. Japan's policy is that individual labourers and workers will set low compensation levels and then take profit sharing when times are good. They take real losses through a reduction in that profit sharing-loss sharing if you will- when times are bad.
Which of those alternatives is the Hon. Member suggesting is appropriate for Canada? Which one does he think that the Canadian Labour Congress and the Canadian labour movement in general would be willing to accept as an alternative to what we have now in this country?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, unfortunately I believe the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) missed the point that I was making with reference to those two countries. I was making the point that both Sweden and Japan have what we might call an economic recovery program in place. They have an industrial and an economic strategy in place so that everyone in those two countries understands clearly what it is the Government of their country is attempting to do. The Governments then ask the people to join in along with the banks, labour and corporations.
What we lack in our country is any idea what it is we are trying to achieve. We lack any direction. The Government simply says, "Let us pick on the Public Service sector and ask that sector to take a reduction in wages. That is our answer."
That was the point I was trying to make, Mr. Speaker. We have, if you will, a rather simplistic approach to economic recovery, and identify only a small, single sector of our society. We say to it, "You must carry the burden; you must carry the can". That is exactly what we should not be doing. If we had a very clear recovery program in place, then, I believe, we would be in a position to go to the various individuals and sectors of society to ask them to join in. But to ask people to join in a recovery program that no one understands or knows, I think, is asking a little bit too much.

Mr. Speaker, I understand what the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) is saying with respect to social justice being achieved through economic development. I presume we all understand that we are all consumers in this country and that we have producers. We will not produce anything unless we can get goods consumed. There is no other way of accumulating production and creating employment unless the goods can be delivered to consumers.
I might say that I agree with the Bishops' statement in which they exposed the problem. That is why I suggested to
the House at one point that we invite the Bishops. But my problem with them really is the solution. How do you achieve what is being talked about? One talks about co-operatives, increased production, job security, and at the same time about reduced inflation. We have been trying to achieve all of these industrial strategies. The Government has been doing that and we are doing our best to achieve those goals. I would like the Hon. Member to tell me of any other proper proposals. Also I would have liked the Bishops to tell us how we can achieve these ends in ways other than the ones we are employing now.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-THE ECONOMY ADVICE OF CANADIAN CONFERENCE OF CATHOLIC BISHOPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me say that subsequent speakers from the New Democratic Party will be laying out precise suggestions in terms of the problems I have indicated. With all due respect to the Hon. Member asking the question, I am suggesting that it is not a matter of simply coming up with a number of suggestions, solutions or alternatives. The Bishops are questioning the assumptions we make in the country.
Let me simply identify one of the assumptions. I believe that most people in this room would say that the overwhelming motive in our economy is the maximization of profits. That is why people are in business and we have corporations. The idea-and we see it played out on a daily basis-is to maximize profits. The question the Bishops are asking is whether or not that should be the ultimate goal rather than the dignity of the citizens of Canada and the people participating in those enterprises.
That is not a criticism about the profit motive or the concept of profits. It is a criticism of the concept of the maximization of profits at the expense of human beings. I am from central British Columbia where mining plays a very critical role in our economy. I have seen mining companies treat human beings as if they were pieces of machinery and have no concern at all about their welfare. If the maximization of profits is beginning to erode, then 200, 300 or 500 men are simply ignored and the welfare of the particular community is totally ignored.
The Bishops are saying that we have to approach this differently, that we have to say, when a mine gets into difficulty and its maximization of profits is not as high as it would like, that there are ultimate strategies which could be built in.
I will return to the country to which I referred earlier. Sweden says to its mining companies that it has a program according to which in good times when they are maximizing their profits they will put some of them into a special fund so that during a period when their profits start to erode they can draw upon the fund and stockpile with Government assistance. In other words, there are a number of things which could be done to enable the community to stay in place and to enable those workers to receive paycheques and provide for their families, not what we see time and time again, that is, simply brute and crass ignoring of the human factor in the economy.
That is the assumption about which we are talking. Any recovery or proposal must take that assumption into consideration. That is what the Bishops are talking about, that we
April 15, 1983

should question some of the assumptions we make about the economy we have come to know in this country.

speechtext:
I do not know what was the intervention of the Hon. Postmaster General, but I hope we will hear from him today before the debate concludes.
I for one welcome the Bishops' statement. I welcome it as a catalyst for focusing public opinion on what is, in my view, the most serious problem facing the country today since the Second World War, that is, an unprecedented unemployment rate since the great depression. If the Bishops have done nothing else but to focus attention and public debate on this, they have fulfilled a great need. Surely it must be obvious to everyone that debate in the House is certainly no longer
Supply
relevant in terms of stimulating public opinion or public debate. Indeed, one only has to look around the House today in the midst of this debate to see a dramatic exemplification of that fact.
If the Bishops are to be faulted on anything, it is on the wording of their statement. For example, I do not believe it was their intention to take the side of labour over management. I do not believe it was their intention to come out in favour of the communist system over the capitalist system, although the wording of the statement has a dangerous tendency to point in that direction. I believe the Bishops were trying to focus attention on the social consequences of a very serious problem. I do not necessarily agree with everything they said, but I certainly agree with their right to say it. I respect their right to say it and I, for one, am glad that they have said it.
I think what the Bishops were concerned about was perhaps best expressed in the paragraph of their statement dealing with the social consequences of high and long-term unemployment. It read:
At the same time, we have seen the social realities of abandoned one-industry towns, depleting unemployment insurance benefits, cut-backs in health and social services, and line-ups at local soup kitchens.
It continued:
And, we have also witnessed, first hand, the results of a troubled economy: personal tragedies, emotional strain, loss of human dignity, family breakdown, and even suicide.
I believe this is what prompted the Bishops to make their unprecedented statement in the first instance. Nobody can quarrel with their right to express that concern. Indeed, it was a concern that was supported by virtually all the Christian churches in Canada. If I recall correctly, the Primate of the Anglican Church made a supportive statement. The moderator of the United Church came out in support of what the Catholic Bishops were trying to achieve. The Presbyterian Church of Canada was supportive of what the Catholic Bishops were tring to focus attention on. Virtually all, if I can say it without being disrespectful, the mainline Christian churches in Canada supported the statement of the Bishops.
This is interesting and significant. The reason they did so was that we have a social crisis in the country of unprecedented proportions. One only has to look at and analyse the unemployment figures-unemployed heads of families, an increase of almost 42 per cent from March of last year. In March, 1982, there were 388,000 unemployed heads of families. In March, 1983, there were 550,000. There was an increase of 31.7 per cent in the number of unemployed women over March of last year. We now have 622,000 unemployed women in this country.
We then come to the long-term unemployed, which goes to the very root and pith and substance of the Bishops' concern, the plight of the long-term unemployed. There was an increase of 80 per cent over March of last year when there were
505,000	Canadians listed as long-term unemployed. As of

April 15, 1983
Supply
March of this year, that figure had jumped to 907,000 out of a total of 1.6 million unemployed. What is a person classed as long-term unemployed? Very simply, it is someone who has been unemployed for three and a half months or more. Generally speaking, we are talking about the exhaustee, the person unemployed so long that his or her Unemployment Insurance benefits have expired. I will return to that in a moment.
Let us continue with our analysis of the unemployment figures for March of this year. There was an increase of 26.2 per cent in the number of young people unemployed over March of last year. In March of last year, there were 492,000 young people unemployed. Young people, as defined by Stats Can, are those between the ages of 15 and 24. That figure jumped to 621,000 in March of this year. This is on the eve of another half million young people coming on the job market from our universities and post-secondary institutions with no hope in the world of obtaining jobs.
If I can be personal for a moment, yesterday there were two young people in my office, both having obtained their Master's degree with majors in Government Administration, both bilingual, indeed one with a working knowledge of Spanish and German. These people have no job prospects. They were excited as all get-out, proud as could be of their accomplishments, with every right to be proud and every expectation to be excited, but what are their prospects for a job? Virtually nil. Therein is the tragedy of our country. We cannot fulfil the expectations of these bright young Canadians coming on to the job market. Within a very short time we will have over one million young people without jobs or job prospects.
We then come to the bottom of the list, the discouraged worker. I can speak with a great deal of feeling about the discouraged worker. I come from a Province that now has an official unemployment rate of almost 21 per cent. Therefore, I have firsthand experience with the problems of the discouraged worker.
During the course of the Easter recess, every day I had these people come to my office, hopeless in their plight, no fuel to heat their homes. Many had no food to put on the table for their families because they could not qualify for welfare payments. The Province had to cut back because of the tremendous demand for welfare.
What do we have in this country in terms of discouraged workers, those who have given up, those with no job prospects? Statistics Canada does not even include them among the unemployed because they have given up. There has been an increase of 30.4 per cent from March of last year. In March, 1982 there were 92,000 discouraged workers. Today there are more that 120,000 discouraged workers with no job prospects.
What kind of country have we presented to our young people? What kind of prospects have we developed for young people coming on to the job market when we have so many discouraged people unemployed, so many who are classified as long-term unemployed?
What has been the Government's response? I believe the lack of a response by the Government prompted the Bishops to
intervene in the first instance. Let us take one facet of the Government's response which deals with those in "dire straits". Who are these people in dire straits? We are told by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that nobody in dire straits in this country will suffer.
According to the Government, those in dire straits are persons who are classified as Unemployment Insurance exhaustees, those who have no Unemployment Insurance. They are coming on to the statistics rolls at anywhere from
60,000	to 100,000 a month in the way of response.
We have the NEED program, a program calling for the expenditure of $500 million. Let us look at what the NEED program has produced since it commenced in November of last year. To date it has produced 3,267 projects for a total of 32,273 jobs, at a total expenditure of $188 million. We spent $188 million to create 32,273 jobs to satisfy the Government's conscience in terms of dealing with those in dire straits, the Unemployment Insurance exhaustees, those coming on to the statistics rolls every month their Unemployment Insurance benefits having expired.
Is it any wonder that the Bishops of Canada found it necessary to make the statement they did at the beginning of this year? As leaders of a major Christian community in this country, in all conscience they had an obligation to speak out, and speak out they did.
When you look at the welfare rolls of the country, you see 1.8 million Canadians who are not even classified in terms of the unemployed because that is a separate statistical data altogether. There are 1.8 million Canadians who depend upon welfare at this time, a significant increase over last year. Where are these people who depend upon welfare? Many of them are in Provinces which had to cut back on welfare because of the 50 cent Canada Assistance Plan dollar. Because the Provinces had to cut back on welfare, they have had to be more discriminatory in terms of who gets welfare and who does not. The result has been genuine hardship in this country. That speaks to the obligation of the Government which created the situation in the first place by its monetarist policy. That was responsible for the loss of half a million jobs since the recession began. The Member can laugh, but the direct consequence of the Government's monetarist policy has been the loss of 550,000 jobs since the recession started.
We have to replace those jobs before we can even address the problems of the long-term unemployed, those coming on to the job market, the young people and native people. After two months, we finally succeeded in getting the Government to strike the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration. It is not without coincidence that this Committee did not meet in the midst of the Bishops' statement, in the midst of the monthly unfolding of these unemployment figures. I propose, as one of the first acts of that Committee, to call the Bishops before the Committee so that they can further explain their position and directly address their concerns to the Parliament of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the time of the luncheon adjournment I was reviewing the climate in which the Catholic Bishops of Canada made what could, I suppose, be described as their precedent-setting statement on the state of the Canadian economy. I was referring to the unemployment situation in Canada as it affects different groups, particularly the plight of the long-term unemployed. I was about to speak on the subject of the Government's response to the serious unemployment situation, especially to the plight of the long-term unemployed, those in dire straits, those who are now described as "exhaus-tees" and no longer qualify for unemployment insurance. The Government's response to the exhaustee situation-although I dislike that term-or those in dire straits, was the NEED Program which was introduced in November, 1982 and which has a budget of $500 million. This Program has created to date 32,273 jobs at an expenditure of $188 million. I believe that the best potential for job creation in this country lies with the private sector and with stimulation of the private sector. 1 understand that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) may be moving in that direction although we will have to wait and see, certainly until the budget is brought down on Tuesday next.
I would like to put forward a proposal which I believe will be less costly and far more productive in terms of job creation than the Government's NEED Program. It is not a new innovation. It is a program which has been tried and has not been found wanting. Indeed, it has been successful. I refer, Mr. Speaker, to employment tax credits.
It is interesting to look at the brief experience we have had with employment tax credits, and I refer to the Economic Council of Canada in its report entitled "In short supply, jobs and skills in the 80's". According to them, the program when it was in effect for a short time, created 50,000 jobs for an expenditure of $100 million. What we have to bear in mind, however, is that these were 50,000 permanent jobs, not 32,273 make-work temporary jobs at a cost of $188 million. These were 50,000 permanent jobs created at a cost of $100 million. The employment tax credit program is a simple, clean, straightforward proposition. Its great advantage is that it can be targeted to meet the needs of various sectors of the work force. For example, it can be used effectively to deal with the problem of the high rate of youth unemployment. It can be
Supply
used effectively with the problem of long-term unemployment, and it can certainly be used and targeted to deal specifically with the problem of exhaustees or those in dire straits.
What we are talking about in Canada today, Mr. Speaker, is not an unemployment rate of 12.6 per cent. If you take into account the 1.6 million Canadians who are seasonally unemployed, the seasonally-adjusted unemployment, and if you add to that figure the 149,000 discouraged workers who are not counted as part of the unemployed, and if you add to that the
407,000	part-time workers or under-employed workers, those who are working under the various make work programs you come up with a real unemployment rate of 2,143,000, or a real rate of unemployment in this country of 18.3 per cent. That, Mr. Speaker, is a very, very serious problem.
I would like to conclude by quoting from the Bishop's report. I hope that it will be possible for them to come before the parliamentary committee. I can think of no better way of summing up than to quote from their report as follows:
There is nothing "normal" or "natural" about present unemployment rates. Indeed, massive unemployment which deprives people of the dignity of human work and an adequate family income, constitutes a social evil.
It is that concern which prompted the Bishops to make their statement in the first instance. It is that concern which prompts this debate in the House today. Hopefully, it will be that same concern which will prompt the Minister of Finance to act when he brings down his budget on Tuesday next.
