speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-THE ECONOMY ADVICE OF CANADIAN CONFERENCE OF CATHOLIC BISHOPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my response will generally reflect the Government's position on the motion presented by the Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis).
As I started to say earlier, Mr. Speaker, Parliamentarians on this side of the House agree with the comments made by the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops. However, to avoid any confusion in this debate, I think it is important to point out right away that all Members, on whatever side of the House they are sitting, in fact every one in general is aware of the very serious problems we are having with unemployment. I do not think anyone is going to downplay this problem. Everyone is aware that economically speaking, we in North America, as in all industrialized countries, are experiencing problems that are directly related to major economic changes, which in turn are the result of a host of internal and external factors. At this point, Mr. Speaker, I would like to make myself quite clear, and I hope my message will be correctly understood on both sides of the House as it regards comments on the present situation as reported by the Bishops and by other groups as well. We share their anxiety and we are very sensitive to the problems described by the Bishops.
However, where we must make a distinction is on the procedure for helping people who are affected by the recession and for introducing the economic and social reforms that would bring about full employment. Here, we find a wide range of opinions being put forward and supported by various schools of thought. On both sides of the House, we have people with views on how the recession should be dealt with, either temporarily or permanently. Where these opinions vary most in connection with the Bishops' letter, is on how to deal with the post-recessionary period. How should the rules of the game be changed? Should we take a more Marxist reading of the facts or should our methods be more on the socialist side? Or should we apply more capitalist methods? Should we have a mixed economy with Government involvement or a strictly free enterprise economy? That is a very important point. We on this side of the House are certainly not rejecting out of hand certain proposals made by the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops. However, before deciding in favour of a given measure, we would like to have a meeting to allow the parties to explain, on the one hand, the Government policies that are now being introduced, and on the other hand, the proposals made by the Bishops in their report.
Even within the Conference, there are bishops who disagree on the best way to overcome the recession. I think that here there is a very clear distinction. We on this side of the House think that it is perfectly normal for the bishops to make statements on social and economic problems. It is their duty to do so. But as far as the means to deal with these problems are concerned, there are a number of different concepts, and I
Supply
think this is amply demonstrated by the ideas being expressed on all sides of the House and supported by all kinds of people with degrees in economics. There are about as many proposals for dealing with the recession as there are PhDs!
We must find a compromise solution that will help us progress on an ongoing basis. That is the crux of the problem today. If we look at other countries, we see that when the French elected their new Government, they were counting on socialist measures to provide a solution to their financial problems. After two years, experience has shown that the hoped-for financial miracle did not come through.
We have seen the same phenomenon in the United States. When the present President was elected three years ago, voters were counting on measures that were directly based on a capitalist system and that would steer clear of social measures as much as possible. They are having problems as well, while here in Canada, the Government has tried to use a little of both. Should we therefore opt for a radical change in the rules of the game?
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the question should come from Members opposite, since, when Mr. Clark's Government was in office, it did extend Mr. Bouey's mandate for another seven years following discussions, I presume, with the Governor of the Bank of Canada. Presumably, Mr. Bouey at the time laid out his own guidelines and the information he gave to the then Government, which saw eye to eye with the thinking, the aims and the means advocated by the Governor of the central bank, prompted the Progressive Conservative administration to extend Mr. Bouey's mandate. Well, we too, enlightened by economists of every description led by Mr. Bouey himself, did check to see what could be done to change the system and to improve significantly the lot of Canadian men and women hard hit by the recession.
Mr. Speaker, unless one does not care whether one's partisan colours are showing, one is forced to admit that all countries of the industrialized world are looking for a way out of the doldrums, and we are not going to solve the problem by stating simply that we must accept or reject the proposals advocated by the Conference of Bishops. Of course there is an extremely simple way to solve the problem. All we need do is to reduce drastically our efforts to promote the personal freedoms of Canadians throughout the country, tag nearly every one of them and put them to work on so-called community projects. The result would be a fantastic drop in the unemployment statistics.
However, what makes the real value of a people or a nation? Two factors: first, their freedom within a well-defined economic, social and political structure, second, the work ethic. That is very important. Evidence of that can be seen when we introduce various programs such as NEED or CCDP, projects

April 15, 1983
Supply
which are usually sponsored by organizations and people are free to accept or reject them since nothing is compulsory. Personal freedom is indeed one of the elements of our system.
The question then is: how do we achieve full employment? I think that the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) gave a good answer earlier today. It is a question of a consumer system which is based on profit, on reinvestment, on a wide ranging market. We are living in a market economy. Would the system be any better if our economy were based simply on a closed market, on a rather socializing market where the state would decide where we work? The state will decide where we go, but I am not sure that the answer lies there.
Among other things we heard from the Conference of Bishops, they stated that perhaps we would be well advised to go back to traditional forms of work. Perhaps I ought to define what that means. If we take fishermen as an example-and the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) is quite familiar with that sector - theirs is a traditional form of work, except that if they want to market their products, they have to resort to extremely competitive and modern practices precisely to be able to open up new markets and create jobs. When it comes to farmers, I should think that very few of them would be prepared to revert to the so-called traditional methods. In that respect alone, we should call an important meeting with the Conference of Bishops to establish exactly just what would be the consequences of going back to rather outmoded practices and replace machinery by sheer human strength. I think that it could be the topic of an interesting debate.
A second fact was pointed out following the statement made by the Assembly of bishops, by Monsignor Cauley, Auxiliary Bishop of Montreal, who stated that either the husband or the wife in a married couple should withdraw from the labour market to enable someone with a greater need to take a job. But then you would be infringing on individual rights and freedoms, because both husband and wife are entitled to plan their career and to work. Should the Government legislate to compel one of them to resign for the benefit of the other? I think that those quite important facts of life should be considered before suggesting that any such option should be chosen.
Another factor should be considered. Is private entreprise still relevant, considering the Bishops' message? And if so, under what form? Nothing has been defined as such in the Bishops' message except that it would obviously be important to deal with this issue. On this side of the House, we are not turning down the message delivered by the Assembly of Bishops. On the contrary. We even find that this message is a challenge to the imagination and the spirit of creativity and should be taken up to provide real and continuous assistance to Canadians who want to work. This recession has made us realize that work which used to be considered by Canadians as being an ordeal or almost as some kind of a misfortune, is now
a privilege. I come from a part of the country which has been dangerously plagued by unemployment in private and public companies both involved in the iron industry. In my area, we have Wabush Mine, Quebec Cartier Mining, Iron Ore, and Sidbec also which is a public company. And if they cannot sell their ore, the same decision has to be made whether it is a public or private company, namely workers have to be laid off. If the message of the Bishops were applied to the letter, would it solve this problem? I think that the question has been well put, but that the answer is more difficult to find.
On the other hand, some changes are certainly necessary within our political system. For instance, because of the way the labour market works at the present time, it is very difficult for a young person to get a job since the unions try to protect the workers already in place, which is normal since the basic role of the unions is to protect their members and give them the best income and the best working conditions possible. This is quite normal. However, could we not establish a system of apprenticeship which would allow young people to join the labour market without threatening the jobs of their seniors, of unionized heads of families? I believe that there are openings to consider in this regard. We are willing to do so in cooperation with the unions.
On the side of management, improvements could certainly be made. For instance, what are the five year development plans to private companies? It is very difficult at the present time for politicians and unions to work in good faith. We seem to be playing cat and mouse. Finally, all the cards are rarely put on the table, which means that it is very difficult for everyone to be honest with each other. A lot of strategy is involved and the good will and good faith of workers is often questioned, I believe.
Yet, people want to work. This is self-evident. People want to work, but perhaps there is a lack of imagination and creativity, and instead of each side accusing the other, it would perhaps be better to have labour, management, government and non-organized workers sit down together to determine whether certain aspects of the social contract should be changed because the way the situation is evolving at the present time is truly tragic. Suicide among young people was mentioned this morning. But what about heads of families who not only have no job, but no hope of getting one?
Young people should certainly not be expected to start a family or to acquire permanent assets at the present time! They have no permanent job. The government is extremely sensitive to this situation, but there is no consensus about a solution, not only in Canada, but also in the United States and Europe. Would it be a good thing to import the Swedish or the Japanese system as suggested by the Hon. Member for Kam-loops-Shuswap (M. Riis) this morning? Some things may indeed be possible. But to come up with a motion blaming the government for refusing to accept the Bishops' message, this is
April 15, 1983

unwarranted. We did accept the Bishops' message. And again we say that we would be ready and willing as indeed we said in a letter signed by Members on this side of the House, and perhaps we should have invited other members to sign that letter. That letter did not condemn the Bishops' statement. There is a distinction to be made namely that when the Bishops speak, we assume that as Christian leaders they are referring to matters of faith. But economic problems are not to be confused with ethical ones. There is a line to be drawn between worldly matters and spiritual matters. Nothing more was meant in that respect. And we hope that in the future, Mr. Speaker, the Bishops will again make their views known on various matters, except that when it comes to solutions, as much as we do not have a monopoly on economic truths, neither do the Bishops.
Of course, in both cases it is through an exchange of views that we can arrive at the best understanding possible with respect to the betterment of people of all denominations, and also of people unrelated to any religious group. And at this stage, it is truly important that the difference be clearly established in this House, because after the Bishops put out their message there was some sort of reluctance. But it was never intended that the Government should remain insensitive to that message, and I for one can say that to a large extent my constituency has been socially and economically developed by priests and members of various religious orders. When referring to Schefferville, let us never forget that Monsignor Scheffer came from Ottawa; he was an Oblate priest from Ottawa who went out as a missionary in that vast territory. The Oblate and Eudist priests were everywhere in the Fort Chimo area, the Ungava, the Middle North Shore and the Lower North Shore, and they did a tremendous job, as did the Protestant ministers. And if the North Shore enjoys such high standards socially, politically, culturally and economically, it is thanks to the various religious orders.
So there was never any question of blaming the Bishops for their message. However, Mr. Speaker, before concluding , since I know my time is rapidly coming to an end, I would like to stress the importance of the choices this Government had to make. I for one, in August 1981, wrote a letter to the Prime Minister condemning the high interest rates that were then hovering around 21 and 22 per cent. In addition, ten Members from the Montreal area signed the letter again asking the Prime Minister that more be done for job creation, but we had to operate in the face of those two simultaneous problems, inflation and unemployment. Several Members from this side of the House have said it repeatedly; With inflation, we can always live; with unemployment we cannot. I think that was also clear.
Now we find that thanks to the policies implemented by both the Canadian and American governments, inflation has abated in a dramatic way, and so much the better for this
Supply
country. At the level of job creation, we must do everything we can to create permanent employment. The Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) was quite right in this regard. Programs such as the CDP's and NEED are useful in the short term, but we must do more in the long term. People in northern cities such as Sept-Iles and Port Cartier, just like people in other constituencies want to have permanent jobs for the young people to develop, because our most important shortage is not a shortage of money, but perhaps a shortage of ideas and creativity to make it through the crisis and guarantee that we shall never again be in the same situation. That is the most important, and I believe that we all share the same concern in this regard, namely .. . Mr. Speaker, I do not know if I still have five minutes left, but if I may have another five minutes, I could conclude my comments. Could I have the agreement of the House to go on for a maximum of five minutes?

Mr. Speaker, I have another question for the Parliamentary Secretary. In their statement three or four months ago, the Bishops mentioned that there was no equality in Canada. They said that the poorest 20 per cent of the population receive only 4 per cent of Canadian income while the wealthiest 20 per cent receive about 42 per cent. The Leader of the Liberal Party, Mr. Trudeau, often promised a just society 15 years ago, a society more equitable than during the fifties and sixties, but as mentioned by the Bishops in their challenge to Canadians, our society is still not equitable. There is still a wide gap between the rich and the poor. Why did you not do something to correct the situation during your 15 years in power?
Second, Mr. Speaker, the standard of living in Canada has gone down a lot since the sixties. At that time, Canada had the second highest standard of living in the world. We now have the nineteenth highest. Why? Why did you allow such a situation-

Mr. Speaker, my first answer concerns the fact that the standard of living may have gone down in Canada. I believe that this phenomenon is North American and that it affects every industrialized country. In other words, in terms of purchasing power, we notice in Canada as well as in the United States or still in many European countries the same phenomenon that appeared 15 years ago but if you now consider the value of our Canadian currency as compared with French or Belgian currency, you will find that conditions are still worse in those countries.
Secondly, Mr. Speaker, concerning the just society, if you look at the Department of National Health and Welfare to which is earmarked almost half of the Canadian budget, you will realize the various steps taken to provide more opportunities to the needy. It would take too much time to list all such measures, Mr. Speaker, and perhaps it would be advisable to send such a list to the Members but once again a great number of measures have been taken to help the more needy during the last 15 years.

speechtext: Yes, I should like to ask a brief question, Mr. Speaker. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-THE ECONOMY ADVICE OF CANADIAN CONFERENCE OF CATHOLIC BISHOPS
speechtext: True enough, Mr. Speaker, there is still much to be done, and we should always strive to attain ideal conditions, except that it is unthinkable that we could attain them on a permanent basis so fast. However, if we consider the constant improvement in the Canadian standard of living over previous years, what is actually essential is to try and narrow the gap between the rich and the poor, and such is the challenge that we must now be ready to take up. This is what the Government wants to do. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-THE ECONOMY ADVICE OF CANADIAN CONFERENCE OF CATHOLIC BISHOPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to enter this debate today. The subject of this motion is very important. I am pleased the Bishops came forward with their statement. It causes us to stop for a moment and do some thinking. The title of the Bishops' statement is "Ethical Reflections on the Economic Crisis". It reflects on some of the concerns all of us face. The economic crisis is very important. My and my Party's particular concern relates to youth. By looking at the figures on the youth unemployment, I find today that over 600,000 young Canadians between the ages of 15 and 24 are presently unemployed. We have a very serious crisis on our hands. This crisis becomes even more serious when we look at the number of graduates who will be hitting the streets this summer. They will be looking for employment opportunities and they will be competing with the many unemployed who have been without a job for some time.
I want to take a look at the Bishops' statement and also discuss what I see is the role of the church. I think the Bishops allowed us that opportunity by releasing this statement. I want
Supply
to look at the economic problems that we face in the country, and finally I want to talk about a few of the things I see as possible solutions.
As one looks at the Bishops' statement I find about five separate points that come forward. I will examine them one at a time. The first point in the statement reads:
First, unemployment rather than inflation, should be recognized as the number one problem to be tackled in overcoming the present crisis.
At first blush I would have no problem agreeing with that, with one exception. People on fixed incomes are the ones most seriously affected by inflation. They are the ones whose income is eroded by inflation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-THE ECONOMY ADVICE OF CANADIAN CONFERENCE OF CATHOLIC BISHOPS
speechtext: Order, please. May I ask the Hon. Members at the back of the House to recognize the fact that the Hon. Member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper) has the floor?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-THE ECONOMY ADVICE OF CANADIAN CONFERENCE OF CATHOLIC BISHOPS
speechtext:
The people on fixed incomes are the ones most seriously hurt by inflation. Right now they may be slightly above the poverty level, but if inflation continues, they will end up below the poverty level. That is my concern with the Bishops' first comment.
The second point made in the statement of the Bishops reads in part:
It should include emphasis on increased production, creation of new labour intensive industries for basic needs, and measures to ensure job security for workers.
Essentially, what the Bishops were outlining is that there should be an industrial strategy. I have no difficulty with that. There has to be a consistent plan and a consistent direction that we as Canadians can work toward.
The third point in the statement of the Bishops reads:
Third, a more balanced and equitable program should be developed for reducing and stemming the rate of inflation.
As is obvious from my comments on the first statement, I was glad to see the Bishops' third point because I think the Bishops' first point is significant and important.
The fourth point in the statement of the Bishops reads:
Fourth, greater emphasis should be given to the goal of social responsibility in the current recession.
That sentence cuts right to the nub of the whole problem we face. Our social security systems are being severely taxed, for instance, the funds for Unemployment Insurance. A number of people are running out of those funds and are listed as exhaus-tees, and we can see that we have a very serious problem.
Maybe it is time to be looking at those of us who do not need some benefits who are still receiving them. For example, my wife and I are receiving a child benefit. In our particular salary bracket I do not think we need that benefit. Maybe it is time to stop and examine that question. Perhaps that money should be given to those who have a genuine and serious need. The Government could give that small cheque which comes to me to someone else and as a result we would provide for those desperately in need.

April 15, 1983
Supply
Returning to the Bishops' statement, it reads:
Fifth, labour unions should be asked to play a more decisive and responsible role in developing strategies for economic recovery and employment.
I found that particular statement very interesting. It sprung out of the page and created a great deal of interest because it concerned responsibility. What has been happening in unions and in other areas is that they have been prepared to fight for their own particular interests and concerns, but in fact there has been no sense of responsibility for other individuals for whom they should be working to create a responsible situation. In other words, a union which represents its employees must at the same time have a responsible concern for the corporation for which it works. Then and only then will there be cooperation and some kind of responsible approach to the problems we are facing.
At this point I want to talk a little about the role of the church in this entire area. I think the Bishops' statement brings that to the fore and provides me with an opportunity to look at it. If we look back at the first Christian church, there was a concern about looking after the needs of the poor and the oppressed. We remember that the first apostles were criticized because Armenian widows within the church were not receiving any kind of assistance or protection. They called a meeting and began to complain about it and indicate that they had a problem. The apostles sat down and said that they were right, that there was a very serious problem. They indicated that they would have to appoint a group of people to look after the basic social concerns of members of their society or their organization, the church. In fact, the person they chose was Stephen, the first martyr of the Christian church. It is from that point that we begin to see an emphasis placed upon the responsibility of the church to play a role on behalf of the poor, the needy and the oppressed.
1 speak as a member of a church and as someone who was raised in the church. I feel very strongly that the church should play a very, very responsible role in society, a responsible role in relating to people and in meeting the concerns of individuals. I am afraid that what has begun to happen lately-and I speak for my own church as well-is that we have transferred that basic responsibility which was talked about in the first church back to the Government or the state. For example, in some cases when widows or needy persons come to us, we say that we will help. We call the nearest Government agency, say that we have a particular individual with a problem and ask for help. There is a real need for the church to get back into that responsibility and to assume that role. The state can provide a certain amount of economic assistance, but there is no emotion or encouragement. I think that is a very important part. It is the human element of meeting economic needs. Therefore we need to see the churches move back into that realm of concern or that particular area which I think is so important.
I have some problems with the capital expenditures of churches as institutions. At this particular time they should not be looking at large facilities which take away their capital. They should be looking at the needs of the people who are members of the churches and at the needs of society in general.
To stand up at the podium and speak about the need to help the needy, the poor and the poverty stricken is not good enough. We have to meet with these people on a day to day basis, talk about their concerns and see what we can do to assist them.
Today we are looking at a number of economic problems. The Bishops referred to it as an economic crisis and indicated:
The present recession appears to be symptomatic of a much larger structural crisis in the international system of capitalism.
I read over that statement two or three times. I thought about it, and my conclusion was that that was probably not the problem. The problem facing us is the one about which Christ talked in the first church. Simply it seems to be going across the board, this business of greed and selfishness. That is the one problem that has been consistent throughout all the systems and processes through time.
Then we come to where we are at today. First there was big business. It exploited people. We have all heard the stories of children in the coal mines and of various other abuses. There was a need for co-operation between workers to protect their particular interests. Then we had big unions to give a balance to big business. I do not think that has worked. Now we look at another option, the third one being big Government or the socialist state. If we have big Government and the state distributes wealth, it will take care of big business and big unions. But I do not see it as being a solution at all because it does not address the basic, simple, responsible position of the individual having to be cautious of his relationships with other people and relating to these other people.
As demonstrated by the Bishops' statements and by things I have seen and heard for years now, on the one hand we have the Bishops making a clear and concise defence of their position and their concerns. On the other hand we have business making a clear and concise defence of its concerns and positions. In a sense we have theory on one side and practicality on the other, but there is no meshing of the two. The problem is that we just keep going on in a sort of blind, desperate fashion, achieving very little. In fact we need to sit down and look at some of the problems we are facing on an individual basis and at our responsibilities as individuals.
What do we see as some of the opportunities? One thing the Bishops mentioned was community ownership. This can mean a couple of things. One could be community ownership through public ownership or state ownership. In the other sense it could mean co-operatives. I like the idea of co-operatives. I think they can be a very valuable tool for allowing us as people and individuals to work together as employees and employers. We are all related because labour is of equal importance to management. I think the balance in a cooperative is very essential and very important, but there is another element through which I think we can achieve the same goals, and that is in the area of private ownership. Private ownership with responsible employers and employees can in fact develop a system which is of benefit to all concerned. If we have employers and employees working together
April 15, 1983

co-operatively and in a way which demonstrates their genuine Christian concern for each other, at that point we begin to address the basic problem we in society are facing.
Essentially I believe that big business will not solve our problem. Big unions will not solve our problem. The option we weem to be exploring more and more of big state will not solve our problem. It is still big. It is still impersonal. It is still numbers. It is still statistics. But it is not a genuine personal concern for individual people.
We have to do a little more thinking about these matters and we have genuinely to relate to people. As Members of Parliament that is something on which we have to focus every day. As I said a few moments ago, there are 600,000 or more young Canadians in Canada who are unemployed. Each one of them is a genuine person with a genuine, serious problem. There is no end to the personal spin-off problems which relate to the fact that they cannot find employment. We must relate to the individual.
In conclusion, I want to refer back to something which Christ said. In Chapter 5 of the Book of Matthew, Christ used the demonstration of light and of salt. He said that Christians were to be the salt of the earth and were to be an example. They were to provide flavour, ideas and all sorts of excitement in society. That is what He meant, that we as individuals should provide an example. When we provide that example and relate it one-to-one, we collectively begin to work on and resolve some of these very serious problems.
In conclusion, I thank the Bishops for coming forward with this statement. It has given us a good chance to reflect and think. It has certainly given me that opportunity. We do have some serious problems in this country. We have to start working on them in a charitable and selfless fashion rather than a selfish fashion, which we have designed, worked in and worked so hard toward over the past few years.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Manicouagan (Mr. Maltais) was indeed speaking on behalf of the Goverment, because I do not have very much to add to his statements on principles and practice. However, I shall be making a few comments of my own. I hope the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) will agree with what I am about to say, because I want to point out that the Bishops' letter, as well as the statements made by the Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) concern a subject on which it is difficult to have a consensus. I do not think the opinion of the Liberal Party is particularly homogeneous, or that there is only one way to consider these matters. I am saying that we
Supply
have some leeway in these matters which the Lord's children are entitled to use.
The motion consists of three parts: first, it regrets that the Government rejected the economic policy set forth in the Bishops' letter. That is not the case at all. We do not reject it. We are sufficiently independent to be able to make nuances so that we certainly did not have to either accept or reject outright the contents of the Bishops' letter. So as far as that is concerned, the motion is entirely unacceptable.
The second part of the motion regrets the Government's refusal to adopt the Bishops' specific recommendations on industrial strategy. Once again, sometimes we agree and sometimes we disagree, and we certainly are not going to refuse or to agree to adopt outright the positions put forward in that letter.
Thirdly, the motion deplores our refusal to adopt a community production system, and I imagine that community production is to be seen here as the opposite of capitalist production or State production. As far as I am concerned, it is one production system among many. It may be morally superior to the rest, but I do not think it is so outstanding that we should not consider other systems, and even the Hon. Member himself says in his motion, in the English text: where desirable. In that case, there is no debate, if the production system is the best one "where desirable". There is no debate, because there may very well be situations where such a system would be very desirable and others where it would not be desirable at all, and in the latter case we would not have to adopt it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-THE ECONOMY ADVICE OF CANADIAN CONFERENCE OF CATHOLIC BISHOPS
speechtext: That is the problem!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-THE ECONOMY ADVICE OF CANADIAN CONFERENCE OF CATHOLIC BISHOPS
speechtext:
That is indeed the problem! I am saying this in a friendly way, because I notice that the Members of the New Democratic Party are becoming more realistic in their aspirations. I get the feeling that they are realizing they do not have a monopoly on truth and virtue, and I like that. It was bound to happen.
I am taking part in this debate for several reasons. First of all, it is my turn to mind the store, and I thought I could usefully take advantage of this opportunity to speak to the House. Second, I have a profound though far from servile, respect for the Church and its authorities, and I think they will appreciate that.
Thirdly, I have always taken a lively interest in economic and social development, and especially in what is referred to as industrial strategy, and it should come as no surprise that I have a few things to say about it. I confess to having drafted a few speeches on that subject, particularly around 1972, and quite a few since then. And if, after my political defeat in 1972, I launched a trading firm, it was precisely because I believed that the means of implementing an industrial strategy were important and that the trading firm seemed to me to be

April 15, 1983
Supply
one of those important means which Canada did not have does not now have on a country-wide basis. There are many trading companies but, in my opinion, none has yet left his imprint throughout the country and the world.
As to the letter from the bishops, I regret to say in passing to my Liberal friends that it is regrettable that it sparked a small debate on the relations between the church and the state. I am very sorry because I do not think there is any justification at all for that. With respect to the relations between civilian power and religious power, the Gospel is not very categorical and says simply: Render unto Caesar what belongs to Caesar and unto God what belongs to God. But never does it say exactly what belongs to Ceasar; that complicates the problem somewhat and, indeed, leaves the question practically wide open. So much so that at different times and in different countries, there were different forms of relationship between the church and the state, ranging from theocracy to neutrality and separation; and all that was advocated by very honest followers, very honest young men and young women alike. The way I look at it, as do most Canadians I think, the bishops can say anything they want on any possible and appropriate subject, as long as they do not claim to be infallible. From that viewpoint, therefore, I regret, as does the Hon. Member for Manicouagan (Mr. Maltais), that they do not speak out more often. I would like to hear them more often on social and economic subjects. Particularly from that point of view, for those of us who come from Quebec, they may be overreacting to offset an inordinately opposite trend in the past. Proper balance is required here as in many other things.
Of course, I will pay them more or less attention depending on the subjects they deal with. When it comes to ethical or moral issues, I take off my hat to them, they are outstanding experts. If they tell me to show respect for work, I quite agree. I applaud. However, if they tell me that intellectual or manual work is better than manual or intellectual work, then I put up an argument because it is not a moral issue. I do respect work, but I can respect various forms of work as well as various forms of work structure. If they proclaim that assistance to the needy is a priority, I bow in agreement and again take my hat off to them. I respect that, I am impressed, I cogitate, I meditate, I pray and I will act as well. But if they tell me that such and such form of assistance to the needy is better than such and such other form, if they tell me that the best way to fight against poverty is to create jobs rather than check inflation, I am prepared to argue. I will probably reach a compromise and say: why should we fight against only one evil? Would it not be better to fight against inflation and unemployment at the same time?
So I read the whole letter and I was duly impressed, and like previous speakers, I pay homage to them because their text is very easy to read, it is very impressive, and in my opinion, as the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) said, it
was needed. Someone had to remind us of those things, particularly inasmuch as they relate to the moral issue.

In economic matters, the bishops are amateurs just like every one of us. For my part, I would have liked the letter to contain-

speechtext: A professional amateur!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-THE ECONOMY ADVICE OF CANADIAN CONFERENCE OF CATHOLIC BISHOPS
speechtext:
Yes, and you are also a professional amateur, my friend!
It would have been a good thing if the difference, the line to be drawn between morality and economic theory and practice were more clearly marked and better expressed in the letter. This is what I have to say and as I have already expressed my views to my favorite bishops, it is certainly not a secret.
I would now like to say a few words about the Bishops' industrial strategy and that of His Eminence Riis, the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap. I am speaking not as an expert, but as someone who has some experience because, as I have already said, I have tried to write some statements which I reread at three in the morning and in which I made several extremely polished comments for instance about the difficulty to define what is an industrial strategy. Some will say that it is a comprehensive and specific plan which wraps up all sectors of the economy, including the social and cultural aspects, in the same package. Others will say that this is too pretentious and that an industrial strategy is simply an order of priority offered for consideration. Others still will say: No, an industrial strategy is a choice of means to achieve ends on which there is a consensus. In addition to all that, the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap made a few wonderful comments earlier, such as:
"Now everything is changing rapidly."

And later on, he also said:

"We want a totally new approach."
[ Translation]
We want an industrial strategy. How can we have an industrial strategy which will apply all the time to every country when things are always changing and change may be the only stable value remaining in the world? How can we develop such an industrial strategy? It is absolutely impossible and this is why Canada has had industrial strategies in the past, why it has one now which may not be quite what each one of us would like, and why there will be a different one in the future. These industrial strategies make me think of the
April 15, 1983

prayer we have all said: As it was in the beginning, as it is now and as it will not be forever and ever.
Mr. Speaker, what I want to say is quite obvious. We all know that we can find as many definitions as we want according to the intellectual, moral and economic tendencies and interests of the person who is speaking. So, accordingly, strategy is all a matter of high technology, or growth sectors, on high productivity or labour intensive or resource intensive or capital intensive sectors. Each of those areas is important. What I am trying to stress is greater reliance on experience, flexibility and humility. There is one example that I always like to bring up. In my opinion, the greatest asset of the Japanese industrial strategy, which is the one most frequently referred to, is that it can change overnight. What gives the Japanese industrial strategy its strength is that they have powerful means and mechanisms which allow them to adopt rapidly and concentrate on a sector where changes are needed, while neglecting another which no longer has priority. In my opinion, that is the major aspect of the Japanese industrial strategy.
Now, what about the Bishops' industrial strategy? First of all it is based on an interpretation of the sources of today's global moral disorder. This has been mentioned by the Member for Manicouagan (Mr. Maltais), but I disagree with the terms he used. Since I am almost twice his age, he will allow me the following remark. You do not have to be a Marxist to appreciate the role of the economy in the development of societies and in the surge of moral disorder in particular. The Bishops' analysis is precisely based on economic factors. They refer to the flow of capital, the development of technology, automation, computerization and so on. Following on that analysis, they say that in order to protect capital, the main concern of governments now is, to control wages, services, to maintain order and so on so as to keep capital in the country. And when all this is taken into account, according to the Bishops, the concern for capital takes precedence over the concern for labour. It is one way of looking at it. I found this interesting, but I wondered how much truth there was in it. A curious mind always puts this kind of question to himself. Is it true that today's governments are limiting salary raises and improvement in services? Well, let us say that it has been true for the last year. One cannot justify an economic theory on a single year. It would have to be analysed over a period of several years to be proven accurate. Yet, if we examine such a theory, going back several years, it is not true. Nowadays, the workers, the people have many more social services than they had ten years ago. So, a theory which is only valid over a one year period is not a very strong one. That is what is annoying me in this theory. The Bishops, for whom I have a great deal of respect, call this the crisis of capitalism. Yes, but what ideology is not in crisis today? There is a crisis of socialism as well, a crisis of marxism, a crisis of communism and a crisis of all ideologies one can think of. All this is very interesting, but it is
Supply
questionable. However, it is food for thought, and from this point of view, it is welcome.
Then the Bishops present us with a series of principles they would like to see implemented: social responsibility, cooperation between groups and regions. They would also like us to give top priority to the fight against unemployment as against, I suppose, the fight against inflation. I am naturally curious. I looked at the document, which states that the number one problem right now is unemployment. This means that further along the line the number one problem might be one of capital, or the need for capital. However, if the concern is for the worker, if labour is to be the basic concern, the fight against unemployment should always have priority. Either this is an all-inclusive, an absolute principle, or it is not. If this it is not an absolute principle, then it is a relative one. But after having established the priority of labour principle, how then can they consider situations in which capital should have top priority! I am very ill at ease with that kind of reasoning.
Further on they advocate an anti-inflation policy which is more equitable. They seem to be pressing for some kind of a price control like the one we had with the Anti Inflation Board, which I had the pleasure or displeasure to chair. This also is highly questionable. It is quite possible both to attend mass and to believe that a six and five policy is a better approach to economic restraint than the one advocated by the Anti-Inflation Board. This is interesting, but questionable.
Further on, they say that we should tax investment incomes, refrain from slashing budgets and social services, maintain health services, help the unemployed. And then there is a phrase that I have not appreciated at all, one that I find fault with: "Counter to policies .. .advocated by governments." I did not like that. A distinction should have been made. They should have said: "Not enough" rather than "counter to". And looking at this ... I could recall three pages, five pages of measures taken by this Government in the areas of help for the unemployed, job creation, job maintenance, construction and so forth. It is somewhat boring to be told, "counter to policies advocated by governments". In my view, such a reproach is much too encompassing. And still further on, the Bishops are suggesting measures that are still more specific, some of which I would again like to argue from a viewpoint the opposite of that held by the Bishops. For instance, that kind of concern they have for labour-intensive industries. That also is questionable. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister. Instead of publicly criticizing the Catholic Bishops who have leadership responsibility for half the population in this country, why did the Government, including the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), not deem it fitting and appropriate to meet with the Bishops to discuss their paper?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-THE ECONOMY ADVICE OF CANADIAN CONFERENCE OF CATHOLIC BISHOPS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not keep track of the Prime Minister's agenda, but I remember vividly that he met some very few days before the Bishops' letter came out with the Catholic Bishops. My hon. friend must realize that this document was written by a committee of the Conference-I do not know the exact word-of the Bishops of Canada; it was not a document of the Conference. I recall, and I am sure my colleagues remember also, that the Prime Minister had met with them. However, this is not a document which is addressed to the Government of Canada. This is a document which is addressed to the population. I do not believe that Governments have to react to documents of this type, and answer them item by item. The Hon. Member was, I believe, wise enough and kind enough to put it on the agenda for today's debate, and I thought we had an opportunity to express some of our views on it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-THE ECONOMY ADVICE OF CANADIAN CONFERENCE OF CATHOLIC BISHOPS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister is referring to a meeting which took place with the committee of the Catholic Bishops on the nuclear question before the statement was issued. I would like to put this proposition to the Minister. Is the Minister saying that if a Cabinet committee brings in a decision, that that is not a decision of the Cabinet but merely of the Cabinet committee? That is the thrust of what he is saying in terms of trying to discount what the committee on social policy of the Canadian Catholic Conference of Bishops said by claiming they did not in fact speak for the Bishops. But surely the document is important enough, and the source is important enough, for the Government to sit down and discuss it with the Bishops, and I regret that the Government has not seen fit to do that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-THE ECONOMY ADVICE OF CANADIAN CONFERENCE OF CATHOLIC BISHOPS
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend can regret that. That is all right. I would like to ask him if he has met with his Bishop on the subject. I have. A number of my colleagues have also. That was one way of reacting and expressing our views. I do not believe a formalized meeting was needed to discuss each item. Again, my information and
knowledge is that the Prime Minister had met with a group of Bishops some very few days before this document was printed.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-THE ECONOMY ADVICE OF CANADIAN CONFERENCE OF CATHOLIC BISHOPS
speechtext:
I would like to be present, Mr. Speaker, when the two Hon. Members who last spoke go to confession in front of their priest or their Bishop. It would be interesting. I wonder if the Minister finds it ironic, perhaps deliciously ironic, if I could put it in his words, that in the past the Bishops in Quebec called the Liberals the "rouge Marxists". Now we have a situation where the Liberals are now calling the Bishops Marxists. It is rather deliciously ironic, it seems to me. The Minister did not seem to indicate that there was need of an industrial strategy at all. He spoke of pragmatism, flexibility and humility, all qualities of his Prime Minister who put him into the transport portfolio.
I would like to know if the Minister feels there is need of industrial strategy, or can we just continue to float in the country? Does he not feel that it was inevitable that someone like the Bishops would respond when you have a monetarist policy which tries to squeeze inflation out of the country by putting people, ordinary people who can least afford to fight back, out of work, and which provides pretty big profits for banks and other groups? Does he not think that it was inevitable that we would have the Bishops or church people calling it immoral? Does he not think that we must in fact have an industrial strategy for the future?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-THE ECONOMY ADVICE OF CANADIAN CONFERENCE OF CATHOLIC BISHOPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend is a lawyer and he tends possibly to deform the thoughts of the criminals he happens to speak against. The Hon. Member for Manicouagan (Mr. Maltais) did not say that it was a Marxist document. He said there was a tinge. Perhaps someone can do that and get away with it in the sense that it invokes economic factors as the source and the cause of moral disorder in society. If I had been a Bishop I might have invoked the original sin as one of the causes. The preoccupation might have been slightly different. From that point of view, there is no doubt that the text has an economic philosophical preoccupation which reminds a person that he has already read that kind of preoccupation. All right? That is not being a Marxist. One can think without being stamped in that fashion. I said also that I was in favour of an industrial strategy which would be flexible, with all the words I have used to say it. I have said that I was in favour of an industrial strategy. I did say that, but I am reacting against the thought, the disposition, of some of those who see it as the nec plus ultra, the beginning and end of everything, and someone who thinks that some day some kind of genius, most probably from the New Democratic Party, will produce a document which will be called "The Industrial Strategy for Canada" and everyone will bow, and then the country will be happy forever and ever. That situation does not exist.
If I had the time I would read to my hon. friend some past documents of the NDP describing what an industrial strategy should be and I would show him very clearly that it has said everything on the subject in the past. At one point it was in
April 15, 1983

favour of concentration on the development of natural resources. Today it is on the manufacturing kick. Tomorrow it may adopt a service kick. Your Party has changed all over the place and God be blessed for that. It proves that your intelligence is stronger than the prejudices you entertain.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-THE ECONOMY ADVICE OF CANADIAN CONFERENCE OF CATHOLIC BISHOPS
speechtext: If we have some time left, Mr. Speaker, could the Minister advise us briefly of his findings?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-THE ECONOMY ADVICE OF CANADIAN CONFERENCE OF CATHOLIC BISHOPS
speechtext: It is simply this. An industrial strategy is a very contentious subject. I think that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lumley) is also involved, judging for instance from his recent statement that he had much more confidence in sectorial strategies than in one universal industrial strategy. That is a clever attitude, for surely the approach should vary when dealing with such diverse industries as the shoe, clothing or high-tech industries. I am sure he shares my views as to the importance of the approach. This should be emphasized. I repeat that an industrial strategy for Canada is a sort of ongoing process which never stops-it is not essential but existential-and it varies with the needs. In this context, to think as Members of the NDP and others do that an industrial strategy would cure all ills forever is a myth, and we should recognize it. To return to the Bishops' statement, I was very much impressed by some of the major and significant moral principles, views and recommendations which I found in it. But I also found views and concerns about various aspects of the industrial strategy which are highly questionable and which I just cannot buy. That is normal.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-THE ECONOMY ADVICE OF CANADIAN CONFERENCE OF CATHOLIC BISHOPS
speechtext: Jolly good, jolly good show!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-THE ECONOMY ADVICE OF CANADIAN CONFERENCE OF CATHOLIC BISHOPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Bishops published their statement they sought a public debate on these issues. They have certainly got one going in the country. In the process, as we have seen this afternoon, they have traded their image of promoting a comfortable pew for making the Government benches rather uncomfortable.
To begin with, I want to pay tribute to the Bishops as I separate what they said in the first part of their statement as a critique from the second part, which goes into recommendations. I want to pay tribute to them particularly for the publication of their critique because they made a distinct contribution to understanding the value system in our society which has led to a situation where, as my friend the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) says, we now have 2,143,000 real unemployed, or 18.3 per cent. I wish to pay particular tribute to the chairman of the social committee of the Bishops who produced this statement, Bishop Remi De Roo of Victoria, who in his personal leadership has exemplified a commitment to the gospel values that the Church espouses. It is a commitment to enhancing social justice throughout Canada and the world.
Supply
As I was informed this morning by the offices of the Canadian Conference of Bishops, so far this statement has resulted in literally hundreds of forums and workshops being held across the country as people of diverse religions are examining what the Bishops are saying. I think that is good. One of those forums will be held soon in Toronto under the leadership of Cardinal Carter.
I also want to pay tribute to him for taking the lead in implementing what the Bishops are saying, not just criticizing the state of the economy and lamenting high unemployment, but actually taking concrete steps through the Archdiocese of Toronto where some $4.6 million of the Archdiocese's money will be combined with federal and provincial matching grants to produce a work program for some 700 unemployed people in Toronto. They will be put to work on a vast range of projects. I think that exemplifies the Church coming to grips in a real way with the problems the statement addresses.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there are some weaknesses in the statement. In a moment I will come to what I see as a certain danger arising from the manner in which the statement was prepared. For the moment I will dwell on what the critique is all about and what the Biships are really saying. The heart of their argument is that the present economic realities reveal a moral disorder in our society. We see that in the massive layoffs of workers and depleting Unemployment Insurance benefits, cutbacks in health and social services, all of which constitutes a social evil in the Bishops' eyes. I say Amen to that; they are absolutely right.
But their critique goes beyond the current economic turmoil and is really aimed at the value system in our society. For we have indeed, sir, produced a survival of the fittest society. Our way of life is geared to those who can keep up with the economic system, which demands relentless growth for success. Public policies, well intentioned though they may be, legislate for the healthy of the economic system and then hopes someone takes care of the casualties.
Who are these casualties? The chronically unemployed, the unskilled, the poorly educated, the minority groups of Indians, Metis and Inuit, the disadvantaged, infirm, aged, one-parent families and inhabitants of depressed areas. All of this, sir, has been labelled by the Senate report on poverty, headed by Senator Croll some years ago, as an ugly subculture within Canadian society.
So it is not only the Bishops who are questioning the morality of the theory in which the poor are supposed to be better off when the rich get richer. The Senate report declared that "there is a call to conscience in this land of ours. No matter how we redistribute income, whether by taxation, fiscal arrangements, capital gains, transfer payments or tariffs, in a very short time the same people end up with all the marbles".
That, sir, is but one illustration of serious critiques offered about our society by people who are serious social analysts. Now, I say to the Parliamentary Secretary that he played on

dangerous ground this afternoon, and the Government allowed him to do so. I gave him the opportunity to say whether or not he believed the Bishops' critique was tinged with Marxism. I say clearly and emphatically that it is not a Marxist critique; it is one that many social analysts are offering about our society today.
The Parliamentary Secretary put his own Minister in a difficult position in trying to get him off the hook. 1 believe that to charge the Bishops with a Marxist analysis in what they have said is to reveal a bias for unfettered individualism. If we are going to have a society where the benefits can be applied to the common good, then we will have to put in place not just what the Bishops are saying but what it represents with regard to the church's teachings for at least 100 years.
What the Bishops said in their critique is not essentially new. They get headlines for the manner in which they said it, but the teachings go back to the first social encyclicals of the church, Rerum Novarum in 1890, Quadragesimo Anno some 40 years later, culminating in the most important encyclical of church teachings in modern times, Pacem in Terris, published by Pope John XXIII about 1958. This sets out, not in just a critique but in capsule form, the values which must be put into place and protected by public policy.
This afternoon I want to put on the record the values of Pacem in Terris, which is the antecedent of the Bishops' statement which we are debating this afternoon. It lists a series of human rights as follows:
Every human being is a person, every person has the right to life, to bodily integrity, to food, clothing, shelter, rest, medical care and social services, to security in case of sickness, inability to work, widowhood, old age, unemployment or deprival otherwise of the means of subsistance through no fault of his own. Every one has the right to respect for his person, to his good reputation, the right to freedom in searching for truth and in expressing and communicating his opinions, the right to be informed truthfully about public events, the right to share in the benefits of culture. Everyone has the right to a basic education and to suitable technical and professional training, the right to free initiative in the economic field and the right to work under good working conditions with a proper, just and sufficient wage. Finally, everyone has a right to private property with its accompanying social duties, the rights of residence and freedom of movement, of membership in the human family and the world communities.
That is the end of that quotation from that encyclical, against which we must test public policies to see how good we are at fulfilling those rights and, of course, we can very clearly see, on the whole question of economic justice and benefits, that in putting so many people into unemployment, they have been deprived of basic rights.
This quotation, which is at the heart of Pacem in Terris, found its way into what I would describe as the centrepiece of the Church's teaching on social justice, which is found in the "Constitution of the Church in the Modern World", which was one of the final documents passed at the second Vatican Council in 1965. In there we find, not a manifesto of specific answers to each of the world's ills, but, rather, a pastoral message that the church should put its ideas and values at the service of the human family. It is that approach which has won a sizeable following in the number of international seminars and so on which have examined what the Church taught in
terms of formulating a social teaching which is applicable to the modern world.
We see, in paragraphs 63 to 72 of the "Constitution of the Church in the Modern World", dealing with the socio-economic life, that the dignity of the human person is emphasized. It is stated: "For man is the source, the centre and the purpose of all economic and social life". The council declared that human labour must always be seen in its true dignity and that workers must never be treated as mere automata in the organization of a complex, productive process. What I would like the House to note is that the council stopped short of detailing what economic or political measures should be used to implement this teaching. Having kept the focus sharply on analysis and principles, the council did not impose specific measures which will always vary according to time and place.
We come to the second part of the Canadian Bishops' statement that we are debating here, for we see that they have plunged into specifics and, indeed, controversy. The Bishops wanted to be heard but, in so doing, they have diminished the acceptance of their valuable critique by risking the charge that they have entered into areas in which their competence as economists may provide some hindrance for them.
I just want to touch briefly on three of the areas. Indeed, the drafter of the NDP motion speaks specifically, not only in complimenting the Bishops for their sound economic advice, but also in speaking of the adoption of the specific recommendations which are contained within the Bishops' statement. 1 think that the authors of the Canadian Bishops' statement may be a little nervous at having realized that what they have put forth is being treated as being specific recommendations. However, I will leave that aside, for they did touch on three areas which are of some concern to me, which is why I am unable to give a full backing to the document, as much as I am in favour of the moral teaching, the critique and analysis of where we are as an inspiration for what we ought to be doing to repair the damage done to human beings.
The first area that I mentioned is the way in which they recommended the new forms of taxes on investment income. The Bishops have mentioned this and even advocated it. I feel, as I am sure many Hon. Members of the House do, that the creation of permanent jobs, which is at the heart of the Bishops' message, depends on massive investments which should not be impeded by more taxation. I believe that it is the taxation system of the country which has acted as an impediment to facilitating more and more investment which is at the heart of the creation of long-range, permanent jobs. That is a great debatable point.
I recognize that my friends in the NDP may not be in total agreement with what I have just said. Perhaps that is the point, that when we come into the House of Commons we are prepared to debate these various questions. However, I have some nervousness that the Bishops, putting out gospel values as they do in their critique, move immediately into a situation in which they are recommending higher forms of investment income.
April 15, 1983

Similarly, the Bishops' statement decries megaprojects, saying that they are not in favour of megaprojects. By that they mean large-scale nuclear plants, pipelines and hydroelectric projects. They say these are undesirable economic strategies. I am not so sure about that. I think the case can be made that what the country needs most at the moment is a huge massive project. I am thinking in terms of the CPR transcontinental railway, the Seaway or gas pipelines in the north. Those structures have a tremendous ripple effect throughout our whole economy, not just in the very areas where they are being built, for we know that the pipelines which have been contemplated and have gone down the drain, so to speak, would have produced enormous numbers of jobs right here in the heartland of Canada, in the industrial plants of Ontario. Therefore, I am not so sure that megaprojects are not an answer to the question of permanent jobs.
Similarly, the Bishops scorn the conversion to high-tech industries. I think that we are moving into a whole new modern era in which high-tech industries will be extremely important, and that if Canada fails to move ahead in microelectronics and petrochemicals, we will forfeit trading gains to the fierce international competition which we face here in this country.
I do not want to be too critical of the Bishops for putting out their ideas. However, I am a little bit nervous about the NDP taking those recommendations and making them their own or, vice versa, that we are confronted with a motion which urges the adoption of the specific recommendations of the Bishops. I have just cited three to which many Hon. Members of the House and I would be unable to give assent.
It is precisely because I want the Bishops' critique and their moral teaching to be heard, and I want it to be unfettered by argumentation over their specifics, that I wish the Bishops would continue to put out their teaching and their stand, but that they would do it in such a way that they challenge Hon. Members of the House from all sides to respond to the moral imperatives which the Bishops have a perfect right to be teaching. I rather think that if future statements of the Bishops followed the lead given by the "Constitution of the Chuch in the Modern World" and the encyclicals going back over the past 100 years, giving us pastoral teaching and allowing the specifics to be debated, determining, by a judgment of the political process, what is best at a given time in a given place, the universality and the timeless nature of the teachings of the church would then be enhanced and protected.

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-THE ECONOMY ADVICE OF CANADIAN CONFERENCE OF CATHOLIC BISHOPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I personally welcome the statement from the Bishops. In my opinion it was right and proper for them to make a comment to us in the Government. I thought they had that right as citizens and I believe they have that mandate as a church.
My personal tradition is in an activist Protestant Christian belief. I am from the United Church and at one time I thought seriously about becoming a clergyman in that church. I was
Supply
drawn to the church, as I am to politics, by the opportunity to comment on my society and to work towards its improvement. I think that the same motives have clearly driven the Bishops in this instance. I suggest that it is the duty of the church to speak on the human condition. The Bishops have done so in this paper.
We clearly heard the statements from the Member for Edmonton South (Mr. Roche) when I believe he quite properly quoted from documents setting out the fundamental ideas on social justice that have spurred the Bishops to go on and talk about our economy and our experiences in Canada.
Last week I personally met with one of the Bishops on a panel discussion, which turned out to be a debate although I did not see it as one. However, the audience saw it as so and their questions were posed as if it were a debate. The Bishop on that panel spoke about the moral values reflected in this statement. I talked about the specific steps followed by the Government in our recent activities. This led the chairman of the panel, Professor Gilles Paquette, to say that we had followed a classic behaviour in which the clergyman had taken the highroad and the politician had looked at the short run. I think he was right. I do not see those two avenues as contradictory paths to follow.
In fact, when I looked at the Bishops' statement I also recognized its two distinct parts. I heard the moral message in the beginning and, as I have just said, I appalauded it. I also saw the recipes, as Professor Paquette described them last week, behind their proposed cures. Today we have seen that those specific recipes arising from the concern are legitimate topics for debate and discussion. The recipes are areas where people differ. They in fact reflect different points of view, different experiences and different ideologies on the world.
As always, some people will suggest that the recipe writers should get their facts straight or be ready for an argument and debate once they have given their recipes. But that does not detract from the importance of making the statement in the first place. It also does not detract from the importance of the moral message contained in the earlier part of the Bishops' document.
Generally speaking, I have found that the Bishops and politicians have agreed in their moral concerns. Politicians are also here because of their social conscience. I have discovered from working 20 years as an activist and now in the last couple of years as a Member of Parliament that my colleagues from all Parties are spurred by the highest of motives. It is my judgment that this could not be reflected any better than it was recently in Toronto when the church got together with the Government through its NEED Program with $11 million to provide hundreds of jobs for needy people. We witnessed the church dedicate more than $4.5 million and be matched with funds from political sources, the Ontario and Canadian Governments. It was an example of everyone coming together to try to create an answer to a very pressing problem. I believe this is the common ground between Government action and the Bishops' concern as indicated in their statement. We have

April 15, 1983
Supply
a common concern and we saw in that example a social program that attempted to cure a demonstrable social ill.
As I have said, I believe that my colleagues in the NDP and the Conservative Party as well as my colleagues in the Liberal Party are in the overwhelming majority spurred on by the same imperative to improve our country and follow our own conscience in serving our fellow citizens.
During this recession we have seen the Government act out of these concerns. We have seen four practical steps followed which reflect the moral concern about the recession felt by Members on this side. First, I think we have indicated quite rightly that there are fundamental illnesses in our economy which must be cured. We could not act without addressing those basic facts and saying to the people, for example, that inflation has weakened our country. We could either provide some rubber patches to a leaky tire and attempt to restore the economy in a haphazard fashion, or we could address the very illness itself. I think it is imperative that we address the illness and cure it. That is what we have said should be the first step.
Second, we have said that we all must bear the burden during difficult times. We have not attempted to hide the fact that there are no magic answers during tough times. There is only hard work to get out of it. We have said that those who have the capacity should help get all of society out of trouble. We have been very clear on that issue.
Third, we have said that we will take the limited resources which we do have and direct them to the people who are most in need. While the vast majority will be asked to use their own resources, those who are most in trouble will receive help where they most need it.
Finally, we have said that it is acceptable, especially during tough times, to use the communities' resources and the Government's spending power to pull the whole country and specific people out of trouble.
I think that these four principles recognize that our country is part of the world and cannot exist in isolation no matter how hard we may want to try. It is not reasonable to try to isolate ourselves from events happening around the world.
We have seen this in my own riding in which there is a company called McDonnell Douglas. I am told that they have one of the most sophisticated machine shops for making aircraft in the world. They make the wings for DC-9s and DC-10s. During the past couple of years airlines have not been purchasing DC-9s or DC-10s and the only choice for the company was to stockpile the wings, which would not be reasonable, or to seek out new orders and aggressively rebuild. The company chose the latter course and DC-9s and DC-10s are being built again today. It would not have been reasonable for the company to fill warehouses full of DC-9 wings out of some misguided principle that we are an isolated autonomy.
Some of our hon. friends from British Columbia are in the House. They have seen the same impact on the lumber industry as a result of the decline in the American housing market. Our colleagues in Ontario and Quebec know the same impact
has hit the mining industry and they know of the experiences we have had in cities like Sudbury. We export and we trade abroad. We are open and subject to these forces that come in on us from the outside world. This is our greatest strength and it would be necessary for us to protect our trading openness, not to close it during times of economic difficulty. We do not want to close our borders. We do not want a magic solution that would tighten up our economy. We want to make sure that the whole world keeps trade as open as possible so that we can deal outward into that world for our own good.
I think the approach the Government is taking recognizes that our fundamental economic trouble can be solved by common effort. We can get our house in order and when the problems in the outside world are solved we will be ready to take advantage. That was the thrust of our six and five program.

And we reached out to big businesses like Chrysler and Massey-Ferguson because their impact was so significant for the whole economy. We have no apologies for helping big or small business when the whole country prospers as a result. Not only do the workers prosper but so do small businesses, other businesses, individual operators and communities who rely on these large operations as well as small ones. We reached out to the farmers last June through the $400 million addition that we put into the Farm Credit Corporation.
We have seen this Government reach out to those most in need while we asked others to try to use their own resources to make do. This has been the area of the greatest dispute. Has the Government been able to do enough? Should the Government do more? Has the Government been spending too much? Should the Government spend less? These are the questions where the heart of the political debate on the recession has taken place. I welcome suggestions that would make us a more effective administrator of all of these programs.

speechtext:
I think if we had instead not increased our deficit, if we had not continued our spending and if we had not been concerned about our social programs, our economy would have been even flatter had we followed the advice of those who said our deficit was too high. Instead we used the deficit. The deficit, or Government spending, is a synonym for community resources and for Canada's resources. We used Canada's resources as a way to cushion those people about whom we have just spoken and who are most in need. We used those resources to spread out the hard times through time, to borrow against the time when the recovery comes and prosperity is returned. We borrowed from those more prosperous future times in order to give ourselves a bit of leeway and provide a bit of stimulus to our economy today.
Supply
Those are the actions the Government has taken in response to some pretty tough economic times. I think they arise out of the same sense of moral concern reflected in the early part of the Bishops' statement. I think we should welcome those statements. We need more of them, not only from the Bishops who have given us a moral imperative, but we also need lots of this kind of feedback from business people who can give us a very practical kind of recipe for our behaviour. We need to hear constantly and regularly from labour and co-operatives who can tell us very often, in as sophisticated a way as we can invent for ourselves, what we need to do to repair our economy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-THE ECONOMY ADVICE OF CANADIAN CONFERENCE OF CATHOLIC BISHOPS
